CHAPTER 13: MAXANNE - WHEN FRIENDSHIP STARTED DYING
**First Person - Maxanne's Voice, Studio B, 2024**
**Word Count Target:** 1,500-2,000 words

---

Three hours left.

The demo tape sits on the console beside me, its label faded but still legible in the amber booth light: "Demo - Nick/Jackie - un-Authorized - March 1979." Forty-five years of sitting in a filing cabinet, waiting for someone to remember that two kids almost made it. The plastic case is warm from my hands—I keep picking it up, putting it down, picking it up again like a rosary bead worn smooth by decades of unanswered prayers.

The ON AIR sign blinks red. The kid in the engineering booth scrolls through his phone, probably texting his girlfriend that he's stuck babysitting some old lady's final show. He has no idea what failure sounds like when it's been fermenting for forty-five years.

I take a sip of bourbon—just one, because getting drunk would be too easy, and I've never done easy—and lean into the microphone.

"You know what nobody tells you about discovering talent?" I say. "They don't tell you that sometimes you find lightning in a bottle and you still can't make it strike twice. They don't tell you that you can have the ear, the instinct, the track record of breaking bands that go on to fill stadiums, and it still won't matter. Because some stories don't end with record deals and tour buses. Some stories end with two kids who had everything it takes, except the one thing you can't manufacture: the ability to survive America's machinery of division."

I spin my chair to face the wall of albums. Aerosmith's first pressing, before anyone knew who they were. The Cars' demo, before they had a label. Boston's early tracks, before Tom Scholz built his basement studio into something legendary. Every one of these bands had something in common—I played them when nobody else would, and they remembered. Steven Tyler still sends bourbon. Ric Ocasek sent a Christmas card every year until he died. These are the wins you hang your career on, the proof that you know what you're doing.

Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh should be on this wall.

They're not.

"November 14th, 1977," I say, and the date tastes like metal in my mouth, like blood from a bitten tongue. "Dan Johnson died on a construction site in Marlborough. Crane cable snapped, and forty-three years of building things with his hands ended in the time it takes to draw a breath. The Globe gave it three paragraphs on page six, wedged between a car accident on Route 9 and a house fire in Framingham. That's what a working man's death is worth in print—three paragraphs and a misspelled last name."

The engineering kid looks up from his phone. Maybe something in my voice cut through his comfortable distance.

"Dan's son Nick was seventeen. Same age as the century when the first World War started—old enough to fight, too young to understand what you're fighting for. Grace Johnson went back to work the next day because the mortgage doesn't care that your husband's gone. She came home from double shifts at Friendly's smelling like fryer oil and forced cheerfulness, and she never once complained that her son spent grocery money on guitar strings. Some people think poverty is just about not having money. It's about not having the luxury to grieve properly. It's about carrying your dead in silence because nobody's listening anyway."

I pick up the tape again. The weight of it feels wrong—too light for what it represents, like holding a bird's hollow bones and being told this thing used to fly.

"Nick stopped playing guitar after Dan died. Just stopped cold, the way you stop speaking a language when there's nobody left who understands it. Every chord reminded him of his father's calloused hands guiding his fingers, every song became a eulogy he wasn't ready to write. That garage on Dutton Road went silent except for the sound of tools nobody would ever use again gathering dust."

Outside the booth windows, Boston glitters in the October darkness. Luxury condos where dive bars used to breed the next generation of bands who'd change everything. Clean streets where dangerous music used to spill out of basement clubs at 2 AM, making everyone who heard it feel like they'd witnessed something that mattered. The city's been gentrified into obedience, and I've been watching it happen for fifty years like a slow-motion funeral.

"Jackie Marsh tried to help," I continue. "God knows he tried. He called, he stopped by, he offered to do homework together or just sit in that garage and not talk. But grief builds walls faster than friendship can climb them. Nick pushed him away with the kind of viciousness that comes from not knowing how to ask for help, from learning too young that the world doesn't stop breaking your heart just because you ask it nicely."

The words come easier now, like lancing an old wound.

"'I don't need your pity,' Nick told him once. I know because Jackie told me years later, and the way he said it—like he was confessing a sin—made me understand that some sentences never stop echoing. 'I don't need anything from you.' Four words that built a wall higher than Hop Brook ever could."

I can see it playing out in my mind like a movie I've watched too many times: Jackie standing in that garage doorway, his college-prep clothes clean and perfect, his face trying to hide how much it hurt to be rejected by someone he'd once harmonized with so perfectly it made teachers cry. Nick surrounded by his dead father's tools, wearing that rejection like armor because armor was the only thing standing between him and complete collapse.

"Jackie didn't understand—how could he? His father was alive and writing papers about the working class without ever having to be working class. His family was intact, his future mapped out in ways that included safety nets and second chances. He wanted to help, but wanting isn't the same as knowing how. And Nick couldn't explain that accepting help from Jackie felt like admitting the gap between them was real, was permanent, was the kind of chasm that swallows friendships whole."

The silence in the booth feels heavy. I let it breathe, the way I learned decades ago that sometimes dead air says more than any song could.

"By the spring of 1978, they'd stopped even pretending. They'd see each other in the hallways at Lincoln-Sudbury, exchange the kind of nod you give strangers, then disappear back into their separate worlds. The cafeteria became a map of everything wrong with America—kids divided by property values and zip codes, by whose parents had to work double shifts and whose parents had summer houses. Nick sat with the working-class kids who knew what it meant to be one paycheck from disaster. Jackie sat with the college-bound crowd who treated SAT scores like they were measuring your worth as a human being."

I look at the clock. Three hours and twelve minutes left. Not enough time to undo what happened, but enough time to bear witness.

"The music that once connected them became the language of their separation. Nick threw himself into Aerosmith—raw, gritty, working-class rock that felt like survival. Jackie doubled down on Queen—theatrical, technically perfect, the sound of someone trying to prove that excellence could transcend origin. They were both right. They were both wrong. Music was supposed to be the bridge, but they'd turned it into ammunition."

The engineering kid is watching me now, phone forgotten. Maybe he's starting to understand that this isn't nostalgia—it's autopsy.

"I've spent forty-five years thinking about Nick and Jackie," I say, and my voice cracks just slightly on Jackie's name. "Thinking about what I could have done differently, what I should have seen coming, whether there was a moment I could have intervened and changed the trajectory. I discovered Aerosmith in 1973. I broke The Cars when they were still playing dive bars in Cambridge. I gave Boston their first airtime when everyone else thought they were too polished, too perfect, too different. I had the touch, the instinct, the reputation for picking winners."

I set the tape down carefully, precisely, like it might shatter.

"But I couldn't save Nick and Jackie. I couldn't make them see what I saw—that together, they had something rarer than talent, rarer than technical skill, rarer than the kind of raw authenticity that music industry people are always chasing. They had balance. They had contrast that created harmony instead of discord. They had the yin-yang chemistry that makes legends, the kind of creative tension that produces art instead of just music."

The booth feels smaller now, like the walls are closing in with the weight of everything I'm about to say.

"And here's what I've learned in the forty-five years since I met them: Division always wins. Always. It doesn't matter how talented you are, how much potential you have, how perfectly your voices blend when you sing together. America's machinery of separation is stronger than any individual connection. We build our suburbs to keep the classes apart. We design our school systems to ensure kids stay in their proper lanes. We create a thousand invisible barriers and then act surprised when people can't cross them."

Outside, a siren wails past on Boylston Street. Emergency on its way to someone's crisis, the sound swallowed by the city's indifferent hum.

"This station closes in three hours," I say. "WBCN, The Rock of Boston, fifty-six years of discovering bands and breaking artists and believing that music could matter more than marketing budgets. We're being shut down so this frequency can be repurposed for automated Christian contemporary, because apparently Jesus sells better than rock and roll. That's the same machinery that pulled Nick and Jackie apart—the force that says connection doesn't matter as much as profit, that harmony loses to division every single time, that the things worth preserving are exactly the things that get erased first."

I pick up the tape one more time. Hold it up to the booth light like I'm examining an X-ray, looking for the fracture point, the moment where everything went wrong.

"But before this station goes dark forever, before I walk out of this booth for the last time and let the corporate suits flip the switch on fifty-six years of music history, I'm going to tell you what happened to Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh. I'm going to tell you about the Battle of the Bands that became a war. I'm going to play you this tape—the only recording that exists of them playing together, the unauthorized demo they cut five days after everything fell apart, the proof that harmony was still possible even after America convinced them they were enemies."

The ON AIR sign pulses like a heartbeat that's running out of time.

"But first, you need to understand how completely their friendship died. You need to know about a wooden bridge over Hop Brook in the fall of 1978, and the day two boys who once made music that could break your heart learned that some divisions can't be bridged. You need to hear about the moment when childhood ended and America's class war claimed two more casualties."

I lean back in my chair. The leather creaks like old bones settling.

"Because the thing about losing something beautiful is this: You have to remember exactly what it looked like before it was gone. Otherwise, you'll forget it was ever possible in the first place. And forgetting—that's the real tragedy. That's what lets division win, over and over, generation after generation. We forget that harmony existed. We forget that different voices once blended into something bigger than themselves. We forget, and then we're doomed to repeat the same damn story until nobody remembers there was ever another way to live."

Three hours and seven minutes left. Just enough time to remember everything.

"The bridge over Hop Brook," I say, and the words taste like goodbye. "That's where we're going next. That's where childhood ended for Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh, and where I learned that sometimes the most talented people in the room still lose. Not because they weren't good enough—but because America's machinery of division is stronger than any two kids with guitars could ever be."

The clock ticks. The city glitters. The station dies in slow motion.

And all I can do is tell the truth before the lights go out.

CHAPTER 14: THE BRIDGE WHERE FRIENDSHIP DIED
**Third Person - Fall 1978**
**Word Count Target:** 2,000-2,500 words

---

Fall 1978, nearly a year after Dan Johnson died, and the friendship between Nick and Jackie had become a casualty they both refused to acknowledge. They nodded in hallways. They didn't speak. The easy intimacy that once let them finish each other's sentences had calcified into the kind of distance that feels permanent.

Nick had learned to carry his grief alone. Jackie had learned that some people don't want to be saved.

And then came the day that made it final.

Saturday afternoon in October, the kind of New England fall day that gets photographed for tourist brochures—leaves bleeding gold and red, air sharp enough to sting your lungs, the conservation land behind Lincoln-Sudbury alive with the sound of dirt bikes tearing through trails that were never meant for engines.

Nick led the pack on a Honda CR125 he'd rebuilt from scrap parts, the two-stroke engine screaming defiance through the woods. Behind him, Carl Dukowski and two other Rollers followed, their bikes idling with the confidence of kids who knew how to fix what they broke.

Jackie was in the woods too, but on foot. He'd been walking these paths since childhood, knew every stone wall marking some dead farmer's ambition. He went there to think, to escape being Richard Marsh's son, to breathe air that didn't smell like expectation.

They met where the main trail crossed Hop Brook.

The wooden bridge was older than either family's time in Sudbury, planks gray with age and slick with moss. Jackie stood dead center, looking down at the water like it might offer answers. Nick killed his engine but didn't dismount, front tire inches from Jackie's boots.

Neither one moved.

"You need to move," Nick said.

"It's a walking bridge," Jackie replied, not looking up. "Always has been."

Behind Nick, the other bikes idled. Their riders sensed this was about more than right of way.

"Lot of things used to be different," Nick said. "Doesn't mean they can't change."

Jackie finally looked up. For a moment—just a flash—they almost smiled at each other. Almost remembered being thirteen and fearless, making music in that garage before the world taught them they were supposed to be enemies.

Then a voice called from the woods. "Everything okay here?"

Dr. Richard Marsh emerged from the trail in pressed khakis and a Boston University windbreaker, dressed for his afternoon constitutional. He took in the scene—his son facing down four kids on dirt bikes—and his face set into an expression that said his worst assumptions were being confirmed.

"These boys bothering you, son?"

And there it was. *These boys.* Not classmates, not neighbors, not even kids. *These boys.* The pronoun that built walls.

"No, Dad," Jackie said, and something in his voice changed. The almost-smile vanished, replaced by the mask he wore at recitals. "I was just explaining about the walking bridge."

Dr. Marsh looked at Nick the way you'd look at a stray dog in your yard—assessment without recognition, threat calculation without seeing a person. In that look lived every letter to the town council, every property value concern, every fear that the wrong element was getting too close.

"Perhaps you boys could find another trail," he said. "One more appropriate for your vehicles."

Nick's hands tightened on the handlebars. Behind him, someone gunned their engine—not threatening exactly, but not not threatening either.

"It's a public trail," Nick said. "We got as much right—"

"Rights," Dr. Marsh interrupted, "come with responsibilities. Something you might understand when you're older."

The casual cruelty of it—the way adults could weaponize class difference with such pedestrian efficiency, turning teenagers into combatants with a single condescending sentence.

What happened next set everything in motion.

Jackie moved. Stepped aside, gave ground, chose peace over principle. The gesture was small—just a few steps to the right—but in the economy of teenage pride, it was surrender.

Nick could have just ridden past. Could have taken the victory and moved on. But something in the way Dr. Marsh stood there—protective and possessive and so goddamn sure of his righteousness—made that impossible.

Nick revved his engine and rode across that bridge at full throttle.

The old wood groaned like something dying. The sound echoed across the water, a scream turned into splinters. His friends followed, four bikes turning the walking bridge into a statement about whose freedom mattered more, whose world had the right to take up space.

When they were gone, the silence felt like aftermath. Like something had been killed that couldn't be brought back.

Dr. Marsh put his hand on Jackie's shoulder. Not comforting—claiming.

"Those boys," he said again, the pronoun carrying even more weight now. "They don't understand boundaries. That's why they'll never amount to anything."

Jackie opened his mouth, then closed it. What could he say? That one of those boys had been his best friend? That they'd made music together that felt like truth? That the boundary wasn't about bridges or trails but about something neither of them had chosen and both were trapped by?

"Come on," Dr. Marsh said. "Your mother's expecting us for dinner."

Jackie looked back once. His eyes met Nick's across the distance that had opened up between them—a distance measured in more than feet, more than the width of Hop Brook, more than the space between their separate quadrants of Sudbury. For a moment, it seemed like he might say something. Might try to bridge what was breaking.

But Dr. Marsh's hand tightened on his shoulder, and Jackie turned away. He followed his father down the trail toward a future already mapped out, toward a world where he belonged and Nick didn't, toward a life that would never include the friendship they'd once shared.

Nick watched them go, understanding that this was it. The friendship was over. Not dying—dead. Done. Whatever they'd had in that garage, whatever harmony they'd found at camp, whatever made them believe music could matter more than money—it was gone.

He sat on his bike for a long time, listening to water flow under the bridge. Thinking about Dan. About that garage full of unused tools. About the music that had once connected them and now just reminded him of everything he'd lost.

Some walls, once built, can't be torn down. Some divisions, once made, become permanent.

He kick-started the engine and rode away, leaving the bridge behind. Leaving Jackie behind. Leaving whatever they'd been to each other behind.

That was it. Four bikes, one pronoun, and a friendship dissolved into the water below.

**Third Person - Fall 1978**
**Word Count Target:** 2,000-2,500 words

---

Fall 1978, nearly a year after Dan Johnson died, and the friendship between Nick and Jackie had become a casualty they both refused to acknowledge. They nodded in hallways. They didn't speak. The easy intimacy that once let them finish each other's sentences had calcified into the kind of distance that feels permanent.

Nick had learned to carry his grief alone. Jackie had learned that some people don't want to be saved.

And then came the day that made it final.

Saturday afternoon in October, the kind of New England fall day that gets photographed for tourist brochures—leaves bleeding gold and red, air sharp enough to sting your lungs. The conservation land that separated the two neighborhoods and ran adjacent to Hop Brook was alive with the sound of dirt bikes tearing through trails that were never meant for engines.

Nick led the pack on a Honda CR125 he'd rebuilt from scrap parts, the two-stroke engine screaming defiance through the woods. Behind him, Stephen Murphy and Mark Pianka—his bandmates from Lincoln—followed on their own bikes, engines idling with the confidence of kids who knew how to fix what they broke.

Jackie was in the woods too, but on foot. He'd been walking these paths since childhood, knew every stone wall marking some dead farmer's claim. He went there to think, to escape his father's house, to be nobody for a while.

They met where the main trail crossed Hop Brook.

The wooden bridge was older than either family's time in Sudbury, planks gray with age and slick with moss. Jackie stood dead center, looking down at the water like it might offer answers. Nick killed his engine but didn't dismount, front tire inches from Jackie's boots.

Neither one moved.

"You need to move," Nick said.

"It's a walking bridge," Jackie replied, not looking up. "Always has been."

Behind Nick, the other bikes idled. Their riders sensed this was about more than right of way.

"Lot of things used to be different," Nick said. "Doesn't mean they can't change."

Jackie finally looked up. For a moment—just a flash—they almost smiled at each other. Almost remembered being thirteen and fearless, making music in that garage before the world taught them they were supposed to be enemies.

Then a voice called from the woods. "Everything okay here?"

Dr. Richard Marsh emerged from the trail in pressed khakis and a Boston University windbreaker, dressed for his afternoon walk. He took in the scene—his son facing down four kids on dirt bikes—and his face set into an expression that said his worst assumptions were being confirmed.

"These boys bothering you, son?"

And there it was. *These boys.* Not classmates, not neighbors, not even kids. *These boys.* The pronoun that built walls. ((** means Italics?))

"No, Dad," Jackie said, and something in his voice changed. The almost-smile vanished, replaced by the mask he wore at recitals. "I was just explaining about the walking bridge."

Dr. Marsh looked at Nick the way you'd look at a stray dog in your yard—assessment without recognition, threat calculation without seeing a person. In that look lived every letter to the town council, every property value concern, every fear that the wrong element was getting too close.

"Perhaps you boys could find another trail," he said. "One more appropriate for your vehicles."

Nick's hands tightened on the handlebars. Behind him, someone gunned their engine—not threatening exactly, but not not threatening either((I think we could siplify maybe something revved his engine, unclear if this was meant to be threatening or not, okay that is too wordy but you get my point i think)).

"It's a public trail," Nick said. "We got as much right—"

"Rights," Dr. Marsh interrupted, "come with responsibilities. Something you might understand when you're older."

The casual cruelty of it—the way adults could weaponize class difference with such pedestrian efficiency, turning teenagers into combatants with a single condescending sentence.

What happened next set everything in motion.

Jackie moved. Stepped aside, gave ground, chose peace over principle. The gesture was small—just a few steps to the right—but in the economy of teenage pride, it was surrender.

Nick could have just ridden past. Could have taken the victory and moved on. But something in the way Dr. Marsh stood there—protective and possessive and so goddamn sure of his righteousness—made that impossible.

Nick revved his engine and rode across that bridge at full throttle.

The old wood groaned like something dying. The sound echoed across the water, a scream turned into splinters. His friends followed, four bikes turning the walking bridge into a statement about whose freedom mattered more, whose world had the right to take up space.

When they were gone, the silence felt like aftermath. Like something had been killed that couldn't be brought back.

Dr. Marsh put his hand on Jackie's shoulder. Not comforting—claiming.

"Those boys," he said again, the pronoun carrying even more weight now. "They don't understand boundaries. That's why they'll never amount to anything."

Jackie opened his mouth, ((what about instead of "then closed it" we write, "but nothing came out" or this could be a chance for a sharp prose like the deadm man referemce ))then closed it. What could he say? That one of those boys had been his best friend? That they'd made music together that felt like truth? That the boundary wasn't about bridges or trails but about something neither of them had chosen and both were trapped by?

"Come on," Dr. Marsh said. "Your mother's expecting us for dinner."

Jackie looked back once. His eyes met Nick's across the distance that had opened up between them—a distance measured in more than feet, more than the width of Hop Brook, more than the space between their separate quadrants of Sudbury. For a moment, it seemed like he might say something. Might try to bridge what was breaking.

But Dr. Marsh's hand tightened on his shoulder, and Jackie turned away. He followed his father down the trail toward a future already mapped out, toward a world where he belonged and Nick didn't, toward a life that would never include the friendship they'd once shared.

Nick watched them go, understanding that this was it. The friendship was over. Not dying—dead. Done. Whatever they'd had in that garage, whatever harmony they'd found at camp, whatever made them believe music could matter more than money ((I don't think money is the right word.  its more than money )) —it was gone.

He sat on his bike for a long time, listening to water flow under the bridge. Thinking about Dan. About that garage full of unused tools. About the music that had once connected them and now just reminded him of everything he'd lost.

Some walls, once built, can't be torn down. Some divisions, once made, become permanent.((maybe reference the old stone walls in the conservation land walls that had been there that pre-dated the Constitution (or some other better reference)))

He kick-started the engine and rode away, leaving the bridge behind. Leaving Jackie behind. Leaving whatever they'd been to each other behind.  

That was it. Four bikes, one pronoun, and a friendship dissolved into the water below.

---

**END CHAPTER 14**

**Word Count:** ~1,050 words
**Status:** READY FOR REVIEW

---

**NOTES:**
- Fixed timeline: Fall 1978 (one year after Dan's death)
- Fixed headers: Chapter 14 consistent
- Nuked ALL "frequency" references
- Removed Maxanne's POV intrusions (pure third person)
- Cut purple prose and repetition
- Tightened to Russo/Lehane directness
- Shortened monster 80-word sentence
- Added killer lines: "calcified into distance," "scream turned into splinters," "claiming not comforting," "walls once built can't be torn down"
- Bridge scene kept strong, opening/closing sharpened
- Ready for your ((comments))

Nick's hands tightened on the handlebars. Behind him, someone revved their engine—the meaning unclear.

"Rights," Dr. Marsh interrupted, "come with responsibilities. Something you might understand when you're older."

The casual cruelty of it—the way adults could weaponize class difference with such pedestrian efficiency, turning teenagers into combatants with a single condescending sentence.

What happened next set everything in motion.

Jackie moved. Stepped aside, gave ground, chose peace over principle. The gesture was small—just a few steps to the right—but in the economy of teenage pride, it was surrender.

Nick revved his engine and rode across that bridge at full throttle.

But Dr. Marsh's hand tightened on his shoulder, and Jackie turned away. He followed his father down the trail toward a future already mapped out, toward a world where he belonged and Nick didn't, toward a life that would never include the friendship they'd once shared.

Nick watched them go, understanding that this was it. The friendship was over. Not dying—dead. Done. Whatever they'd had in that garage, whatever harmony they'd found at camp, whatever made them believe music could bridge the gap between their worlds—it was gone.

He sat on his bike for a long time, listening to water flow under the bridge. Thinking about Dan. About that garage full of unused tools. About the music that had once connected them and now just reminded him of everything he'd lost.

Fall 1978, nearly a year after Dan Johnson died, and the friendship between Nick and Jackie had become a casualty they both refused to acknowledge. They nodded in hallways. They didn't speak. The easy intimacy that once let them finish each other's sentences had calcified into the kind of distance that feels permanent.

Nick had learned to carry his grief alone. Jackie had learned that some people don't want to be saved.

And then came the day that made it final.

Saturday afternoon in October, the kind of New England fall day that gets photographed for tourist brochures—leaves bleeding gold and red, air sharp enough to sting your lungs. The conservation land that separated the two neighborhoods and ran adjacent to Hop Brook was alive with the sound of dirt bikes tearing through trails that were never meant for engines.

Nick led the pack on a Honda CR125 he'd rebuilt from scrap parts, the two-stroke engine screaming defiance through the woods. Behind him, Stephen Murphy and Mark Pianka—his bandmates from Lincoln—followed on their own bikes, engines idling with the confidence of kids who knew how to fix what they broke.

Jackie was in the woods too, but on foot. He'd been walking these paths since childhood, knew every stone wall marking some dead farmer's claim. He went there to think, to escape his father's house, to be nobody for a while.

They met where the main trail crossed Hop Brook.

The wooden bridge was older than either family's time in Sudbury, planks gray with age and slick with moss. Jackie stood dead center, looking down at the water like it might offer answers. Nick killed his engine but didn't dismount, front tire inches from Jackie's boots.

Neither one moved.

"You need to move," Nick said.

"It's a walking bridge," Jackie replied, not looking up. "Always has been."

Behind Nick, the other bikes idled. Their riders sensed this was about more than right of way.

"Lot of things used to be different," Nick said. "Doesn't mean they can't change."

Jackie finally looked up. For a moment—just a flash—they almost smiled at each other. Almost remembered being thirteen and fearless, making music in that garage before the world taught them they were supposed to be enemies.

Then a voice called from the woods. "Everything okay here?"

Dr. Richard Marsh emerged from the trail in pressed khakis and a Boston University windbreaker, dressed for his afternoon walk. He took in the scene—his son facing down four kids on dirt bikes—and his face set into an expression that said his worst assumptions were being confirmed.

"These boys bothering you, son?"

And there it was. *These boys.* Not classmates, not neighbors, not even kids. *These boys.* The pronoun that built walls.

"No, Dad," Jackie said, and something in his voice changed. The almost-smile vanished, replaced by the mask he wore at recitals. "I was just explaining about the walking bridge."

Dr. Marsh looked at Nick the way you'd look at a stray dog in your yard—assessment without recognition, threat calculation without seeing a person. In that look lived every letter to the town council, every property value concern, every fear that the wrong element was getting too close.

When they were gone, the silence felt like aftermath. Like something had been killed that couldn't be brought back.

Dr. Marsh put his hand on Jackie's shoulder. Not comforting—claiming.

"Those boys," he said again, the pronoun carrying even more weight now. "They don't understand boundaries. That's why they'll never amount to anything."

Jackie opened his mouth, but the words died in his throat like fish pulled from water. What could he say? That one of those boys had been his best friend? That they'd made music together that felt like truth? That the boundary wasn't about bridges or trails but about something neither of them had chosen and both were trapped by?

"Come on," Dr. Marsh said. "Your mother's expecting us for dinner."

Jackie looked back once. His eyes met Nick's across the distance that had opened up between them—a distance measured in more than feet, more than the width of Hop Brook, more than the space between their separate quadrants of Sudbury. For a moment, it seemed like he might say something. Might try to bridge what was breaking.

But Dr. Marsh's hand tightened on his shoulder, and Jackie turned away. He followed his father down the trail toward a future already mapped out, toward a world where he belonged and Nick didn't, toward a life that would never include the friendship they'd once shared.

Nick watched them go, understanding that this was it. The friendship was over. Not dying—dead. Done. Whatever they'd had in that garage, whatever harmony they'd found at camp, whatever made them believe music could bridge the gap between their worlds—it was gone.

He sat on his bike for a long time, listening to water flow under the bridge. Thinking about Dan. About that garage full of unused tools. About the music that had once connected them and now just reminded him of everything he'd lost.

Some walls last longer than the people who build them. The stone walls in these woods had outlived the farmers who stacked them, still dividing land nobody owned anymore. Some divisions, once made, become permanent.

He kick-started the engine and rode away, leaving the bridge behind. Leaving Jackie behind. Leaving whatever they'd been to each other behind.  

That was it. Four bikes, one pronoun, and a friendship dissolved into the water below.

```plaintext
CHAPTER 15: THE POSTER
**Third Person - April 2, 1979**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

April 2nd, 1979. A Monday morning that changed everything.

The Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School music room occupied a corner of the building where acoustics went to die. Cinder block walls painted institution green, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, instrument lockers that hadn't been properly maintained in years. But on the bulletin board between the jazz band schedule and a faded Boston Symphony poster, someone had mounted something new.

**BATTLE OF THE BANDS**  
**May 15, 1979**  
**Open to all regional high schools**  
**Grand Prize: $500 and professional recording session**  
**Sponsored by WBCN "The Rock of Boston"**

Five hundred dollars in 1979 was real money. Three months of Grace Johnson's grocery budget. A used car. A semester at community college. For Nick, it was boots without duct tape, maybe a guitar with strings that didn't snap mid-song. For Jackie, it was validation that couldn't be bought, proof that talent mattered more than his father's money.

Bob Wentworth found them both standing there at 7:47 AM, staring at the poster from opposite sides of the room. Wentworth had given up symphony halls for steady paychecks twenty years ago, but he could still hear potential in the noise teenagers made.

"Gentlemen," he said. "I see you've noticed the announcement."

Neither boy moved. They stared at that poster like it might answer questions they'd been carrying for months.

"Band names due Friday," Wentworth continued. "Performance slots are limited to eight bands."

That's when Nick looked at Jackie. Really looked at him for the first time since the bridge.

Jackie had grown into what Nick expected—tall, clean, clothes that fit perfectly. Hair that fell across his forehead in that effortless way that cost money. He looked like someone who'd never worried about the electricity staying on.

Nick had hardened. His clothes were worn but clean, boots resoled with duct tape, hands showing calluses from weekend work at the auto shop. He looked like someone who'd never treated music as anything but escape.

"I suppose you'll both be entering," Wentworth said into the silence.

"Queen tribute," Jackie said. Not a suggestion—a challenge.

"Aerosmith," Nick countered.

Wentworth sighed. "The competition is meant to celebrate musical diversity—"

"It's about proving who's real," Nick interrupted. "Who understands what rock and roll actually means."

"It's about excellence," Jackie shot back. "About showing that rock can be more than three chords and attitude."

Wentworth looked from one boy to the other, understanding this went beyond music. This was about proving something fundamental about who they were.

"Gentlemen," Wentworth said carefully. "I attended the '75 Curtis Middle School Talent Show. You brought the house down together."

He pulled a photograph from his desk drawer—two thirteen-year-old boys, arms around each other, holding guitars. Smiling like they owned the world.

"This is what you were capable of," Wentworth said, holding it up.

Nick and Jackie stared at the photograph. For a moment, it seemed like they might remember. Might recognize who they'd been before the world taught them to be enemies.

But Nick looked away first. Jackie followed.

"That was then," Nick said, his voice flat. "This is now."

"Working-class kids can make music that matters," Nick continued. "You don't need expensive instruments or fancy training to create something real."

"Excellence isn't negotiable," Jackie countered. "Rock and roll can be more than garage band noise."

Wentworth watched the friendship die again, right there in front of him.

By lunch, the entire school knew.

It wasn't Nick Johnson versus Jackie Marsh anymore. It was working class versus privilege, garage rock versus conservatory training, Aerosmith versus Queen. The cafeteria became a battlefield of musical taste—kids who'd never cared about music suddenly had opinions about production values and authenticity.

The Lincoln kids lined up behind Nick like a militia forming. The Sudbury kids split along economic lines, the Hop Brook divide made visible in cafeteria seating. Kids literally moved tables to sit with their chosen side.

Even the teachers took sides. Mr. Ogden referenced Queen's harmonics in physics class. Mrs. Williams hummed Aerosmith while teaching pie crust technique. The janitor just shook his head and kept mopping.

Almost no one knew what Wentworth knew—that in 1975, these two boys had won the middle school talent show as a duo. That at thirteen, they'd stood on that gymnasium stage and made music that left audiences breathless.

The poster hung on that bulletin board for six weeks, turning the high school into a war zone. Kids who'd never spoken suddenly had strong opinions about musical authenticity. Teachers who'd never cared about rock and roll found themselves taking sides. The school newspaper ran a poll: Queen or Aerosmith. Queen won by twenty points. Nick's supporters claimed voter fraud.

And in the middle of it all, two boys who'd once been best friends prepared to prove something to each other, to their school, to themselves. Nick practiced until his fingers bled. Jackie rehearsed until his voice went hoarse.

The Battle of the Bands was six weeks away.

Everyone was choosing sides.

The only question was whether music would bring them together or tear them apart forever.

That at thirteen, they'd stood on a gymnasium stage and created something that made grown adults cry because it was so pure, so honest, so completely free of everything that would come later.

The poster hung on that bulletin board for six weeks. Every morning, students stopped to look at it. Some added notes in the margins—band names, practice schedules, crude drawings of guitars. The paper became worn at the edges from being touched so many times, from being read and reread like it might reveal something new.

And in the middle of it all, two boys who'd once been best friends practiced separately, in different rooms, in different parts of town. Nick worked through "Dream On" until his fingers cramped. Jackie rehearsed "Somebody to Love" until his throat was raw.

Neither one called the other.

Neither one would be the first to give in.

The Battle of the Bands was six weeks away, and Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School was choosing sides in a war that nobody wanted but everybody seemed to need.

Because sometimes the only way to prove you've survived losing something is to compete against what you lost.

And sometimes that's the saddest thing of all.

Five hundred dollars in 1979 was real money. Three months of Grace Johnson's grocery budget. A used car. A semester at community college. For Nick, it meant his mother wouldn't have to pick up that extra Friday shift at Friendly's. For Jackie, it meant proving something his father couldn't buy for him.

Nick entered from the west hallway, heading to his first period class. They both saw the poster at the same moment and moved toward it, reading from opposite sides of the bulletin board. Close enough that their shoulders almost touched. Close enough to remember what it felt like to stand next to each other without everything else in the way.

Bob Wentworth watched from his desk. He'd given up symphony halls for steady paychecks twenty years ago, but he could still hear potential in the noise teenagers made. And he could recognize a dangerous moment when he saw one.

"Gentlemen," he said. "I see you've noticed the announcement."

Neither boy moved. They kept staring at the poster like it might offer a way back to something they'd lost.

"Band names due Friday," Wentworth continued. "Performance slots are limited to eight bands."

That's when Nick looked at Jackie. Really looked at him for the first time since the bridge.

Six months had changed them both. Jackie stood straighter now, like he'd finally grown into the posture his parents had been correcting since childhood. His eyes were careful, measured. Nick's jaw was set in a way that hadn't been there before, his hands still even when they used to fidget. They'd both learned how to hide.

"I suppose you'll both be entering," Wentworth said into the silence.

"Queen," Jackie said. Not a suggestion—a statement of fact.

"Aerosmith," Nick said.

Wentworth sighed. "The competition is meant to celebrate musical diversity—"

"It's about the music," Nick interrupted, still looking at Jackie. Not at Wentworth.

"Exactly," Jackie said. "The music. Not the story around it."

"Right. Just the sound."

"Just what you can actually do."

Wentworth looked from one boy to the other, understanding that every word they were saying meant something else entirely. They weren't talking about music at all. They were talking about everything that had broken between them, everything they'd lost, everything they couldn't say directly because saying it out loud would make it too real.

He wanted to stop this. He'd seen it before—friendships that turned into competitions, competitions that turned into something uglier. But he also knew that some moments couldn't be stopped, only witnessed.

You two stood on that stage together." He found what he was looking for—a photograph, slightly faded. "You made music that mattered ((mattered = corny, find something more real))."

"This is what you were capable of," Wentworth said.

Nick and Jackie stared at the photograph. For a moment, something shifted in both their faces—recognition, maybe, or grief for who they used to be. The room was so quiet Wentworth could hear the clock ticking on the wall.

But Nick looked away first. Jackie followed.

"That was middle school," Nick said, his voice flat. "This is different."

"We're different," Jackie added.

"Yeah," Nick said. "We are."

The bell rang. Students would flood the hallways in thirty seconds.

"I'm entering," Nick said. ((because he didn't know what to saym Nick stated,  "May the best band win.))

CHAPTER 15: THE POSTER

April 2nd, 1979. Monday morning, 7:30 AM.

The Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School music room occupied a small corner of the building where acoustics went to die. Cinder block walls painted institution green, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, instrument lockers that hadn't been properly maintained in years. Music had been dying at L-S for a while now—budget cuts, declining enrollment in electives, kids choosing computer lab over band practice. But on the bulletin board between the jazz band schedule and a faded Boston Symphony poster, someone had mounted something new.

**BATTLE OF THE BANDS**
**May 15, 1979**
**Open to all regional high schools**
**Grand Prize: $500 and professional recording session**
**Sponsored by WBCN "The Rock of Boston"**

Five hundred dollars in 1979 was real money. Three months of Grace Johnson's grocery budget. A used car. A semester at community college. For Nick, it meant his mother wouldn't have to pick up that extra Friday shift at Friendly's. For Jackie, it meant proving something his father couldn't buy for him.

Nick entered from the west hallway, heading to his first period class. Jackie came through the east entrance, dropping off sheet music before homeroom. They both saw the poster at the same moment and moved toward it, reading from opposite sides of the bulletin board. Close enough that their shoulders almost touched. Close enough to remember what it felt like to stand next to each other without everything else in the way.

Bob Wentworth watched from his desk. He'd given up symphony halls for steady paychecks twenty years ago, but he could still hear potential in the noise teenagers made. And he could recognize a dangerous moment when he saw one.

"Gentlemen," he said. "I see you've noticed the announcement."

Neither boy moved. They kept staring at the poster like it might offer a way back to something they'd lost.

"Band names due Friday," Wentworth continued. "Performance slots are limited to eight bands."

That's when Nick looked at Jackie. Really looked at him for the first time since the bridge.

Six months had changed them both. Jackie stood straighter now, like he'd finally grown into the posture his parents had been correcting since childhood. His eyes were careful, measured. Nick's jaw was set in a way that hadn't been there before, his hands still even when they used to fidget. They'd both learned how to hide.

"I suppose you'll both be entering," Wentworth said into the silence.

"Queen," Jackie said. Not a suggestion—a statement of fact.

"Aerosmith," Nick said.

Wentworth sighed. "The competition is meant to celebrate musical diversity—"

"It's about the music," Nick interrupted, still looking at Jackie. Not at Wentworth.

"Exactly," Jackie said. "The music. Not the story around it."

"Right. Just the sound."

"Just what you can actually do."

Wentworth looked from one boy to the other, understanding that every word they were saying meant something else entirely. They weren't talking about music at all. They were talking about everything that had broken between them, everything they'd lost, everything they couldn't say directly because saying it out loud would make it too real.

He wanted to stop this. He'd seen it before—friendships that turned into competitions, competitions that turned into something uglier. But he also knew that some moments couldn't be stopped, only witnessed.

"Wait," Wentworth said carefully, pulling open his desk drawer. "I attended the '75 Curtis Middle School Talent Show. You two stood on that stage together." He found what he was looking for—a photograph, slightly faded. "You made something real."

He held up the photograph. Two thirteen-year-old boys, arms around each other, holding guitars. Smiling like the future was something they'd figured out together.

"This is what you were capable of," Wentworth said.

Nick and Jackie stared at the photograph. For a moment, something shifted in both their faces—recognition, maybe, or grief for who they used to be. The room was so quiet Wentworth could hear the clock ticking on the wall.

But Nick looked away first. Jackie followed.

"That was middle school," Nick said, his voice flat. "This is different."

"We're different," Jackie added.

"Yeah," Nick said. "We are."

The bell rang. Students would flood the hallways in thirty seconds.

"I'm entering," Nick said. ((because he didn't know what to saym Nick stated,  "May the best band win.))

"So am I," Jackie said. (("You can count it" Jackie replie)) ((just as suggestion or find something better, the othe exchange sounds too childlike)) 

They walked out through different doors without looking back. Wentworth sat at his desk, still holding the photograph of two boys who used to be best friends, and felt something break in his chest that he couldn't quite name. He'd seen students lose interest in music, lose passion for their instruments, lose faith in their own talent. But he'd never watched two kids lose each other quite like this—slowly, inevitably, like watching a landslide in slow motion and being unable to stop it.

By lunch, the entire school knew.  ((Here is where we need to work in some subtletys ...)) ((I think we could show that posters now hung not only the music room, but in the library, the cafeteria on the way to the gymnasium even in the infanous smokey Glass Corridors and this created an unexpected buzz.  Music had been dying at the high school years, but this seemed to resuscitate the school's interests.))

The kind of competition that made everyone choose without anyone asking them to. April 2nd, 1979. Monday morning, 7:30 AM.

The Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School music room occupied a small corner of the building where acoustics went to die. Cinder block walls painted institution green, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, instrument lockers that hadn't been properly maintained in years. Music had been dying at L-S for a while now—budget cuts, declining enrollment in electives, kids choosing computer lab over band practice. But on the bulletin board between the jazz band schedule and a faded Boston Symphony poster, someone had mounted something new.

**BATTLE OF THE BANDS**
**May 15, 1979**
**Open to all regional high schools**
**Grand Prize: $500 and professional recording session**
**Sponsored by WBCN "The Rock of Boston"**

Five hundred dollars in 1979 was real money. Three months of Grace Johnson's grocery budget. A used car. A semester at community college. For Nick, it meant his mother wouldn't have to pick up that extra Friday shift at Friendly's. For Jackie, it meant proving something his father couldn't buy for him.

Nick entered from the west hallway, heading to his first period class. Jackie came through the east entrance, dropping off sheet music before homeroom. They both saw the poster at the same moment and moved toward it, reading from opposite sides of the bulletin board. Close enough that their shoulders almost touched. Close enough to remember what it felt like to stand next to each other without everything else in the way.

Bob Wentworth watched from his desk. He'd given up symphony halls for steady paychecks twenty years ago, but he could still hear potential in the noise teenagers made. And he could recognize a dangerous moment when he saw one.

"Gentlemen," he said. "I see you've noticed the announcement."

Neither boy moved. They kept staring at the poster like it might offer a way back to something they'd lost.

"Band names due Friday," Wentworth continued. "Performance slots are limited to eight bands."

That's when Nick looked at Jackie. Really looked at him for the first time since the bridge.

Six months had changed them both. Jackie stood straighter now, like he'd finally grown into the posture his parents had been correcting since childhood. His eyes were careful, measured. Nick's jaw was set in a way that hadn't been there before, his hands still even when they used to fidget. They'd both learned how to hide.

"I suppose you'll both be entering," Wentworth said into the silence.

"Queen," Jackie said. Not a suggestion—a statement of fact.

"Aerosmith," Nick said.

Wentworth sighed. "The competition is meant to celebrate musical diversity—"

"It's about the music," Nick interrupted, still looking at Jackie. Not at Wentworth.

"Exactly," Jackie said. "The music. Not the story around it."

"Right. Just the sound."

"Just what you can actually do."

Wentworth looked from one boy to the other, understanding that every word they were saying meant something else entirely. They weren't talking about music at all. They were talking about everything that had broken between them, everything they'd lost, everything they couldn't say directly because saying it out loud would make it too real.

He wanted to stop this. He'd seen it before—friendships that turned into competitions, competitions that turned into something uglier. But he also knew that some moments couldn't be stopped, only witnessed.

"Wait," Wentworth said carefully, pulling open his desk drawer. "I attended the '75 Curtis Middle School Talent Show. You two stood on that stage together." He found what he was looking for—a photograph, slightly faded. "You made something real."

He held up the photograph. Two thirteen-year-old boys, arms around each other, holding guitars. Smiling like the future was something they'd figured out together.

"This is what you were capable of," Wentworth said.

Nick and Jackie stared at the photograph. For a moment, something shifted in both their faces—recognition, maybe, or grief for who they used to be. The room was so quiet Wentworth could hear the clock ticking on the wall.

But Nick looked away first. Jackie followed.

"That was middle school," Nick said, his voice flat. "This is different."

"We're different," Jackie added.

"Yeah," Nick said. "We are."

The bell rang. Students would flood the hallways in thirty seconds.

"May the best band win," Nick said, because he didn't know what else to say.

"You can count on it," Jackie replied. 

They walked out through different doors without looking back. Wentworth sat at his desk, still holding the photograph of two boys who used to be best friends, and felt something break in his chest that he couldn't quite name. He'd seen students lose interest in music, lose passion for their instruments, lose faith in their own talent. But he'd never watched two kids lose each other quite like this—slowly, inevitably, like watching a landslide in slow motion and being unable to stop it.

By lunch, the entire school knew.

The posters multiplied. Someone—maybe the WBCN intern, maybe a student who worked in the office—had made copies. By second period, they hung in the library. By third, one appeared in the cafeteria near the lunch line. By fourth, there was one taped to the entrance of the gymnasium, another in the infamous Glass Corridors where kids smoked between classes and pretended the teachers couldn't see through the haze.

Music had been dying at L-S for years. But this—a professional competition, a real prize, WBCN sponsorship—woke something up.

It wasn't just Nick Johnson versus Jackie Marsh. It was Aerosmith versus Queen. Garage rock versus private lessons. The kind of competition that made everyone choose without anyone asking them to.

And something strange happened.

Lincoln-Sudbury had always been divided. You were a Ramper—the cool kids, the ones with letter jackets and party invitations. Or you were a Rat—the rebels who smoked in the Glass Corridors and showed up late. Or you were a Reg—regular, invisible, just trying to get through without being noticed. Or you were a Roller—the kids who hung around the auto shop, fixing cars, riding anything with an engine.

Those lines didn't blur. They didn't cross. That was just how it worked.

But the Battle of the Bands did something nobody expected. It created a new division that cut straight through the old ones. Rampers who liked Aerosmith sat with Rats at lunch. Regs who'd never spoken to Rollers argued about Queen's vocal harmonies on the school bus. Kids who couldn't tell the difference between a power chord and a car chord were picking sides anyway, the way you pick a team in a game you don't understand but everyone else is playing.

The four-way split that had defined the school for generations suddenly collapsed into two camps. And for the first time in years—maybe ever—kids from different worlds were talking to each other.

Over the next two weeks, the cafeteria split down the middle. The Lincoln kids gravitated toward Nick's table without discussion, without plan. The Sudbury kids divided themselves—some toward Jackie, some toward Nick—following instincts they couldn't name. Geography older than any of them, playing out in lunch table arrangements.

Kids who'd sat together for years found themselves on opposite sides of an aisle they'd never noticed before. New friendships formed, at least temporarily.

Even the teachers felt it, though they'd never admit it. Mr. Ogden found himself thinking about harmonic structures during ((author change: during calculus class)). Mrs. Williams caught herself humming "Dream On" while demonstrating how to fold pie dough in the home ((ec room)). ((Don't need the next sentence here)) The school secretary started making playlist notes on her desk calendar. The janitor kept his head down and mopped, having seen this kind of thing before and knowing it never ended well. (( last line is good))

Almost no one knew what Wentworth knew—that in 1975 ((i don't think this could be true as all the kids theuy went to moddle school with are now in high school together so would have known at least some of them)), these two boys had won the middle school talent show as a duo. The Sudbury kids divided themselves—some toward Jackie, some toward Nick—following instincts they couldn't name. Geography older than any of them, playing out in lunch table arrangements.

Kids who'd sat together for years found themselves on opposite sides of an aisle they'd never noticed before. New friendships formed, at least temporarily.

Even the teachers felt it, though they'd never admit it. Mr. Ogden found himself thinking about harmonic structures during calculus class. Mrs. Williams caught herself humming "Dream On" while demonstrating how to fold pie dough in the home ec room. The janitor kept his head down and mopped, having seen this kind of thing before and knowing it never ended well.

Few people remembered what Wentworth remembered—that in 1975, these two boys had won the middle school talent show as a duo. Most of their classmates had been there, but four years is a long time when you're seventeen. Memories fade. Friendships end. People forget that things were ever different. That at thirteen, Nick and Jackie had stood on a gymnasium stage and made something that felt honest, pure, completely free of everything that would come later.

The poster ((I would have posters as a plurarl as described above)) hung on that bulletin board for six weeks. Every morning, students stopped to look at it. Some added notes in the margins—band names, practice schedules, crude drawings of guitars. The paper became worn at the edges from being touched so many times, from being read and reread like it might reveal something new.

And in the middle of it all, two boys who'd once been best friends practiced separately, in different rooms, in different parts of town ((take this out as it is unrealistic)). Nick worked through "Dream On" until his fingers cramped. Jackie rehearsed "Somebody to Love" until his throat was raw.  

Neither one called the other.  ((They were way past this point now))

Neither one would be the first to give in.

The Battle of the Bands was six weeks away, and Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School was choosing sides in a war that nobody wanted but everybody seemed to need ((not sure I fully understand this sentence, what did they "need"?)).

Because sometimes the only way to prove you've survived losing something is to compete against what you lost.

And sometimes that's the saddest thing of all. ((okay at least for now))

CHAPTER 15: THE POSTER
**Third Person - April 2, 1979**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

April 2nd, 1979. Monday morning, 7:30 AM.

The Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School music room occupied a small corner of the building where acoustics went to die. Cinder block walls painted institution green, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, instrument lockers that hadn't been properly maintained in years. Music had been dying at L-S for a while now—budget cuts, declining enrollment in electives, kids choosing computer lab over band practice. But on the bulletin board between the jazz band schedule and a faded Boston Symphony poster, someone had mounted something new.

**BATTLE OF THE BANDS**
**May 15, 1979**
**Open to all regional high schools**
**Grand Prize: $500 and professional recording session**
**Sponsored by WBCN "The Rock of Boston"**

Five hundred dollars in 1979 was real money. Three months of Grace Johnson's grocery budget. A used car. A semester at community college. For Nick, it meant his mother wouldn't have to pick up that extra Friday shift at Friendly's. For Jackie, it meant proving something his father couldn't buy for him.

Nick entered from the west hallway, heading to his first period class. Jackie came through the east entrance, dropping off sheet music before homeroom. They both saw the poster at the same moment and moved toward it, reading from opposite sides of the bulletin board. Close enough that their shoulders almost touched. Close enough to remember what it felt like to stand next to each other without everything else in the way.

Bob Wentworth watched from his desk. He'd given up symphony halls for steady paychecks twenty years ago, but he could still hear potential in the noise teenagers made. And he could recognize a dangerous moment when he saw one.

"Gentlemen," he said. "I see you've noticed the announcement."

Neither boy moved. They kept staring at the poster like it might offer a way back to something they'd lost.

"Band names due Friday," Wentworth continued. "Performance slots are limited to eight bands."

That's when Nick looked at Jackie. Really looked at him for the first time since the bridge.

Six months had changed them both. Jackie stood straighter now, like he'd finally grown into the posture his parents had been correcting since childhood. His eyes were careful, measured. Nick's jaw was set in a way that hadn't been there before, his hands still even when they used to fidget. They'd both learned how to hide.

"I suppose you'll both be entering," Wentworth said into the silence.

"Queen," Jackie said. Not a suggestion—a statement of fact.

"Aerosmith," Nick said.

Wentworth sighed. "The competition is meant to celebrate musical diversity—"

"It's about the music," Nick interrupted, still looking at Jackie. Not at Wentworth.

"Exactly," Jackie said. "The music. Not the story around it."

"Right. Just the sound."

"Just what you can actually do."

Wentworth looked from one boy to the other, understanding that every word they were saying meant something else entirely. They weren't talking about music at all. They were talking about everything that had broken between them, everything they'd lost, everything they couldn't say directly because saying it out loud would make it too real.

He wanted to stop this. He'd seen it before—friendships that turned into competitions, competitions that turned into something uglier. But he also knew that some moments couldn't be stopped, only witnessed.

"Wait," Wentworth said carefully, pulling open his desk drawer. "I attended the '75 Curtis Middle School Talent Show. You two stood on that stage together." He found what he was looking for—a photograph, slightly faded. "You made something real."

He held up the photograph. Two thirteen-year-old boys, arms around each other, holding guitars. Smiling like the future was something they'd figured out together.

"This is what you were capable of," Wentworth said.

Nick and Jackie stared at the photograph. For a moment, something shifted in both their faces—recognition, maybe, or grief for who they used to be. The room was so quiet Wentworth could hear the clock ticking on the wall.

But Nick looked away first. Jackie followed.

"That was middle school," Nick said, his voice flat. "This is different."

"We're different," Jackie added.

"Yeah," Nick said. "We are."

The bell rang. Students would flood the hallways in thirty seconds.

"May the best band win," Nick said, because he didn't know what else to say.

"You can count on it," Jackie replied. 

They walked out through different doors without looking back. Wentworth sat at his desk, still holding the photograph of two boys who used to be best friends, and felt something break in his chest that he couldn't quite name. He'd seen students lose interest in music, lose passion for their instruments, lose faith in their own talent. But he'd never watched two kids lose each other quite like this—slowly, inevitably, like watching a landslide in slow motion and being unable to stop it.

By lunch, the entire school knew.

The posters multiplied. Someone—maybe the WBCN intern, maybe a student who worked in the office—had made copies. By second period, they hung in the library. By third, one appeared in the cafeteria near the lunch line. By fourth, there was one taped to the entrance of the gymnasium, another in the infamous Glass Corridors where kids smoked between classes and pretended the teachers couldn't see through the haze.

Music had been dying at L-S for years. But this—a professional competition, a real prize, WBCN sponsorship—woke something up.

It wasn't just Nick Johnson versus Jackie Marsh. It was Aerosmith versus Queen. Garage rock versus private lessons. The kind of competition that made everyone choose without anyone asking them to.

And something strange happened.

Lincoln-Sudbury had always been divided. You were a Ramper—the cool kids, the ones with letter jackets and party invitations. Or you were a Rat—the rebels who smoked in the Glass Corridors and showed up late. Or you were a Reg—regular, invisible, just trying to get through without being noticed. Or you were a Roller—the kids who hung around the auto shop, fixing cars, riding anything with an engine.

Those lines didn't blur. They didn't cross. That was just how it worked.

But the Battle of the Bands did something nobody expected. It created a new division that cut straight through the old ones. Rampers who liked Aerosmith sat with Rats at lunch. Regs who'd never spoken to Rollers argued about Queen's vocal harmonies on the school bus. Kids who couldn't tell the difference between a power chord and a car chord were picking sides anyway, the way you pick a team in a game you don't understand but everyone else is playing.

The four-way split that had defined the school for generations suddenly collapsed into two camps. And for the first time in years—maybe ever—kids from different worlds were talking to each other.

Over the next two weeks, the cafeteria split down the middle. The Lincoln kids gravitated toward Nick's table without discussion, without plan. The Sudbury kids divided themselves—some toward Jackie, some toward Nick—following instincts they couldn't name. Geography older than any of them, playing out in lunch table arrangements.

Kids who'd sat together for years found themselves on opposite sides of an aisle they'd never noticed before. New friendships formed, at least temporarily.

Even the teachers felt it, though they'd never admit it. Mr. Ogden found himself thinking about harmonic structures during calculus class. Mrs. Williams caught herself humming "Dream On" while demonstrating how to fold pie dough in the home ec room. The janitor kept his head down and mopped, having seen this kind of thing before and knowing it never ended well.

Few people remembered what Wentworth remembered—that in 1975, these two boys had won the middle school talent show as a duo. Most of their classmates had been there, but four years is a long time when you're seventeen. Memories fade. Friendships end. People forget that things were ever different. That at thirteen, Nick and Jackie had stood on a gymnasium stage and made something that felt honest, pure, completely free of everything that would come later.

The posters hung everywhere for six weeks. Every morning, students stopped to look at them. Some added notes in the margins—band names, practice schedules, crude drawings of guitars. The paper became worn at the edges from being touched so many times, from being read and reread like they might reveal something new.

And in the middle of it all, two boys who'd once been best friends practiced separately, in different rooms, in different parts of town ((take this out as it is unrealistic)). Nick worked through "Dream On" until his fingers cramped. Jackie rehearsed "Somebody to Love" until his throat was raw.  

Neither one called the other.  ((They were way past this point now))

Neither one would be the first to give in.

The Battle of the Bands was six weeks away, and Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School was choosing sides in a war that nobody wanted but everybody seemed to need ((not sure I fully understand this sentence, what did they "need"?)).

Because sometimes the only way to prove you've survived losing something is to compete against what you lost.

And sometimes that's the saddest thing of all. ((okay at least for now))
