```plaintext
CHAPTER 18: THE TOWN WEIGHS IN
**Third Person - Late April 1979**
**Word Count Target:** 1,500-2,000 words

---

By late April, Sudbury had chosen sides.

Grace Johnson noticed it first at the grocery store. Women she'd known for years now stopped to ask about Nick's "big competition" with a particular tone in their voices—some encouraging, some pitying, all of them making it clear they'd formed opinions about how this would end. The cashier at Star Market asked if Nick was nervous. The pharmacist wanted to know if he was "ready for that kind of pressure." Even Mrs. Warren at the dry cleaners had thoughts about whether garage bands could compete with "proper training."

Grace kept her responses short. "He's working hard." "He's focused." "We'll see what happens."

What she didn't say: *Please stop making my son's high school talent show sound like the rest of his life depends on it.*

---

The Sudbury Diner on Route 20 had become neutral territory, which meant it had become a battlefield. Grace sat in her usual booth Tuesday morning, her one day off from Friendly's, nursing coffee and trying to read the Globe. But the conversations around her made that impossible.

"—real talent versus just making noise—"

"—Marsh kid's been trained since he was five—"

"—but the Johnson boy's got heart, you can hear it—"

"—heart doesn't win competitions—"

Grace kept her eyes on her newspaper. The Red Sox had lost to the Yankees again. Nothing new there.

"Grace?" Mary Murphy slid into the booth across from her without being invited. Her son Stephen played bass in Nick's band. "How's Nick holding up?"

"He's fine."

"Stephen says they're practicing six hours a day. Is that true?"

"Something like that."

Mary leaned forward, voice dropping. "Grace, people are betting on this. Frank at the barber shop has a pool going. My husband put ten dollars on Nick winning."

Grace looked up from her newspaper. "People are betting on high school kids?"

"It's Sudbury," Mary said, as if that explained everything. Maybe it did.

The waitress came by to refill Grace's coffee. She was wearing a button that said "Rock the Vote" with a small Aerosmith logo underneath. Grace hadn't voted for anything. Wasn't planning to.

"The whole town's talking about it," Mary continued. "The Weekly ran another article yesterday. Front page. They interviewed both families. Did you see it?"

Grace had seen it. The reporter had called three times before she'd finally agreed to answer questions. They'd photographed Nick in the garage, surrounded by Dan's tools, looking like exactly what he was—a working-class kid trying to make something out of nothing. The headline: "Battle of the Bands: Two Students, Two Worlds, One Stage."

"I saw it," Grace said.

"Dr. Marsh wasn't happy about that article," Mary said. "My neighbor works at the school. She said he called the principal, wanted to know why they were 'turning a musical competition into class warfare.'" Mary made air quotes with her fingers.

Grace said nothing. Took another sip of coffee.

"There's a PTA meeting Thursday night," Mary said. "Emergency session. About the 'tension' in the school." More air quotes. "Are you going?"

"I work Thursday nights."

"Grace, you should be there. Dr. Marsh is going to be there. He's going to talk about how this whole thing has gotten 'out of hand' and maybe they should cancel the competition to 'restore harmony in the school community.'"

Grace set down her coffee cup carefully. "He wants to cancel it?"

"That's what I heard."

"Two weeks before the Battle?"

"He's going to say it's for the kids' own good. That the competition is causing too much stress, dividing the school, creating an unhealthy environment." Mary leaned back, watching Grace's face. "Someone needs to tell him that's bullshit."

Grace looked at Mary Murphy. They'd known each other for fifteen years. Their sons had played Little League together, gone to the same elementary school, learned to ride bikes in the same neighborhood. Mary's husband worked at the post office. They lived three streets over in a house that looked exactly like Grace's—small, worn, paid for one month at a time.

"I'll be there," Grace said.

---

Thursday night, Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School's library was packed. The PTA had scheduled the meeting for seven, but by six-forty-five every seat was taken. Parents stood along the walls, crowded in the doorway. Principal Sargent sat at the front table looking like he regretted every decision that had led to this moment.

Grace arrived at six-fifty, still wearing her Friendly's uniform. She stood in the back, next to the water fountain.

Dr. Richard Marsh sat in the front row, surrounded by other parents from the northwest part of town. He wore a blazer and khakis. His wife sat beside him, perfectly composed. They looked like people who attended a lot of meetings and knew how to run them.

Principal Sargent called the meeting to order at seven-oh-five. "Thank you all for coming. I know emotions are running high about the upcoming Battle of the Bands competition. The purpose of tonight's meeting is to address concerns about the impact this event is having on our school community."

Dr. Marsh raised his hand. Was recognized immediately.

"Thank you, Brad," he said, using the principal's first name in a way that suggested they'd talked before this meeting. "I think we all want what's best for our children. And I think we can all agree that what started as a simple musical competition has become something else entirely. Students are skipping classes to practice. Arguments are breaking out in hallways. The school newspaper ran a poll asking students to choose sides—as if this were a political election rather than a talent show."

He paused, letting that sink in.

"What concerns me most," Dr. Marsh continued, "is that this competition has become a referendum on class. Working-class students versus privileged students. Garage bands versus classical training. This is not what education should be about. We're supposed to be teaching our children to work together, to respect different approaches, to celebrate diversity. Instead, we're teaching them to compete, to divide, to see each other as adversaries."

Several parents nodded. Someone said, "Hear, hear."

"I propose," Dr. Marsh said, "that we cancel the competition. Or at the very least, postpone it until next fall, when emotions have cooled and we can approach it with the proper educational framework."

More nodding. More murmurs of agreement.

Grace felt something shift in her chest. That old familiar anger—the kind that came from being told by people with money and education what was best for people without either.

"Excuse me." Her voice carried across the library. Heads turned.

Principal Sargent looked relieved to see her. "Grace. Please, come up front."

Grace walked down the center aisle. She was aware of her Friendly's uniform, her worn sneakers, the fact that she smelled like fryer oil no matter how many times she washed. She was aware of Dr. Marsh watching her approach, his expression carefully neutral.

She stood in front of the room. Didn't sit.

"I'm Grace Johnson," she said. "Nick's mother. I work at Friendly's. I couldn't afford to take tonight off, but I'm here anyway because Mary Murphy told me there was talk about canceling the competition my son has been working toward for six weeks."

She looked directly at Dr. Marsh.

"Dr. Marsh is right about one thing. This competition has become about class. But not because the kids made it that way. Because the adults did. Because we decided that some kinds of music matter more than others. That some kinds of training are more legitimate than others. That some kids deserve opportunities and other kids should just be grateful for what they get."

The room was silent.

"My son practices in a garage his father built before he died. He plays a guitar that cost twenty-five dollars at a pawn shop. He's been working weekends at an auto shop to help pay for new strings. This competition—this five-hundred-dollar prize, this recording session—it means something to him. It means his music matters. It means talent comes from more than just expensive lessons and the right neighborhood."

She paused. Took a breath.

"Dr. Marsh wants to cancel the competition because his son might lose. He's dressing it up as concern about education and school harmony, but what he really means is that he can't imagine his son competing on equal ground with someone like mine. Because if Jackie Marsh—with all his training, all his advantages, all his opportunities—if he loses to a kid from a garage in Lincoln ((Sudbury)), what does that say about all the money((don't think we need this line as the next part says it all)) Dr. Marsh has spent? What does that say about the world he believes in, where success goes to the people who can afford it?"

Dr. Marsh stood up. "That's not fair—"

"You're right," Grace said. "It's not fair. None of this is fair. But canceling the competition won't fix that. It'll just teach our kids that when things get hard, when the outcome isn't guaranteed, we give up. We find excuses. We protect the kids who were always going to be fine and tell the others that their dreams are just hobbies."

She looked around the room. At the parents watching her. At Principal Sargent, who was trying not to smile. At Mary Kowalski ((Murphy)) in the back, who gave her a small nod.

"Let them compete," Grace said. "Let them play their music. Let them find out what happens when you work hard and take a chance and put yourself out there. Win or lose, that's worth more than any lesson we could teach them by canceling it."

She walked back down the aisle. Out the door. Into the parking lot.

Her hands were shaking. She sat in her car for a long time before driving home.

---

The PTA voted forty-two to eleven to keep the competition as scheduled.

Grace heard about it later from Mary, who called at ten-thirty that night.

"You should have seen Marsh's face," Mary said. "He tried to respond, tried to say you'd misunderstood him, but nobody wanted to hear it. Principal Sargent called for a vote five minutes after you left. It wasn't even close."

"Good," Grace said.

"Grace, that was the bravest thing I've ever seen."

Grace didn't feel brave. She felt tired. She had to be at Friendly's at six the next morning.

"Get some sleep, Mary," she said, and hung up.

The Battle of the Bands was nine days away.

The whole town was watching.

---

**END CHAPTER 18**

**Word Count:** ~1,900 words
**Status:** READY FOR REVIEW
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 19: GRACE LOSES HER GRACE
**Third Person - May 1, 1979**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

Grace Johnson had been working at Friendly's for twenty-three years. Twenty-three years of polyester uniforms and name tags, of serving coffee to the same people, listening to the same conversations. She'd started in 1956, nineteen and newly married to Dan. What had seemed temporary became permanent. Problems multiplied. And here she was, forty-two, still wearing the same uniform.

The difference was, now she had a son about to compete in the Battle of the Bands. Now she had a son whose future hung in the balance of other people's opinions.

And she was tired of listening.

---

It started with Dr. Patterson in booth twelve, reading the Sudbury Weekly's latest front-page story about the Battle. He looked up when Grace came to refill his coffee.

"I've been reading about this competition," he said. "Quite the controversy."

"Yes, Dr. Patterson." Grace poured carefully.

"I'm concerned about how it's dividing the community. All this talk about class and privilege—it's as if people are using music to air grievances." He leaned forward, taking on the tone he probably used with patients who didn't understand their diagnosis. "Take your son, for example. Nick, isn't it? I've heard he's talented. But this competition is setting up unrealistic expectations. These kids will be disappointed when they realize talent alone isn't enough."

Grace's hand tightened on the coffee pot. "I'm not sure I follow."

"I'm just saying it's important to be realistic. The music industry is very competitive. It takes more than talent—it takes connections, resources, training that costs money. I'm concerned this competition is giving these kids false hope."

Grace set the coffee pot down. Not quite a slam. Not quite gentle either. "Are you suggesting my son shouldn't compete because he doesn't have the right training?"

"No, of course not. I'm just saying that talent alone isn't enough. These competitions can be discouraging for kids without the proper background."

"Proper background." Grace's voice changed. Something Dr. Patterson had never heard in twenty-three years of her serving him coffee. "My son has been playing guitar since he was eight. He practices every day in the garage his father built. He's won every talent show he's entered. WBCN invited him to compete. And you're telling me he doesn't have the proper background?"

Dr. Patterson shifted. "Grace, I didn't mean—"

"What exactly are you suggesting, Dr. Patterson? That my son shouldn't compete because he's not from the right family? Because he doesn't have the right connections?"

"I think you're misunderstanding—"

"I understand perfectly." Grace's voice was steady now. Clear. "You're saying my son shouldn't compete because he's working class. Because his mother's a waitress and his father died in an accident. Because he doesn't have advantages."

Dr. Patterson's face reddened. He looked around the restaurant. Other customers were listening. No one came to his rescue.

"You've been coming here twenty-three years," Grace said. "You've watched me serve you coffee. Listened to your opinions about everything. But you've never once asked about my son's dreams. Never asked about his talent. Now that he's entering a competition that might give him a chance, you're suddenly concerned about 'realistic expectations.'"

"Grace, I was trying to be helpful—"

"You're not being helpful. You're being condescending. You're telling me my son shouldn't compete because if he loses to someone with his background, what does that say about the world you believe in? The one where success goes to people who can afford it?"

Dr. Patterson looked at his coffee cup. "I think we should end this conversation—"

"We're done." Grace straightened her uniform. "Enjoy your pie, Dr. Patterson. It's made from apples grown in this town, served by people who live in this town. Maybe think about that next time you discuss what's realistic."

She walked to the next table—booth seven, young couple sharing dessert—and asked if they needed anything else. Her voice back to professional courtesy. As if nothing had happened. As if she hadn't just demolished the polite fiction that allowed Friendly's to function as neutral territory.

---

The manager, Tom Andrews, called her into the back room twenty minutes later. Fifteen years managing Friendly's, never seen anything like it. He had the conversation managers have with employees who violate the cardinal rule: never make customers uncomfortable with your humanity.

But Tom had grown up in Sudbury. Had worked construction with Dan Johnson. Had been to the funeral. Had watched Grace carry herself through circumstances that would have broken most people.

He gave her a lecture about professionalism and customer relations.

Then he gave her a raise.

Fifteen cents an hour.

Grace didn't know whether to laugh or cry. Fifteen cents for finally saying what everyone knew but pretended they didn't. For proving the help had opinions, feelings, children whose futures mattered.

---

The story spread through Sudbury by Monday morning. Everyone had heard some version of what happened at Friendly's. Details varied depending on who told it and what they needed it to mean.

Some said Grace had been rude to a customer. Some said Dr. Patterson had been condescending to a waitress. Some said it was a misunderstanding. Some said it was about time someone stood up to the attitude that made working-class people feel like they didn't belong in their own town.

Nick heard about it at school. Three different people told him his mom had "gone off" on a customer. He drove straight to Friendly's after practice, found Grace wiping down tables at the end of her shift.

"Mom. I heard—"

"It's fine, Nick."

"Did you really tell off Dr. Patterson?"

Grace looked at her son. Seventeen years old, guitar calluses on his fingers, Dan's eyes. "I told him the truth."

"What truth?"

"That you deserve a chance. Same as anyone."

Nick was quiet for a moment. Then: "You didn't have to do that."

"Yes," Grace said. "I did."

She finished wiping the table. Folded the rag. Untied her apron.

"Come on," she said. "Let's go home."

They walked out together into the parking lot. The Battle of the Bands was eight days away.

---

**Status:** READY FOR REVIEW
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 19: GRACE LOSES HER GRACE
**Third Person - May 1, 1979**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

Grace Johnson had been working at Friendly's for twenty-three years. Twenty-three years of polyester uniforms and name tags, of serving coffee to the same people, listening to the same conversations. She'd started in 1956, nineteen and newly married to Dan. What had seemed temporary became permanent. Problems multiplied. And here she was, forty-two, still wearing the same uniform.

The difference was, now she had a son about to compete in the Battle of the Bands. Now she had a son whose future hung in the balance of other people's opinions.

And she was tired of listening.

---

It started with Dr. Taub in booth twelve, reading the Sudbury Weekly's latest front-page story about the Battle. He looked up when Grace came to refill his coffee.

"I've been reading about this competition," he said. "Quite the controversy."

"Yes, Dr. Taub." Grace poured carefully.

"I'm concerned about how it's dividing the community. All this talk about class and privilege—it's as if people are using music to air grievances." He leaned forward, taking on the tone he probably used with patients who didn't understand their diagnosis. "Take your son, for example. Nick, isn't it? I've heard he's talented. But this competition is setting up unrealistic expectations. These kids will be disappointed when they realize talent alone isn't enough."

Grace's hand tightened on the coffee pot. "I'm not sure I follow."

"I'm just saying it's important to be realistic. The music industry is very competitive. It takes more than talent—it takes connections, resources, training that costs money. I'm concerned this competition is giving these kids false hope."

Grace set the coffee pot down. Not quite a slam. Not quite gentle either. "Are you suggesting my son shouldn't compete because he doesn't have the right training?"

"No, of course not. I'm just saying that talent alone isn't enough. These competitions can be discouraging for kids without the proper background."

"Proper background." Grace's voice changed. Something Dr. Taub had never heard in twenty-three years of her serving him coffee. "My son has been playing guitar since he was eight. He practices every day in the garage his father built. He's won every talent show he's entered. WBCN invited him to compete. And you're telling me he doesn't have the proper background?"

Dr. Taub shifted. "Grace, I didn't mean—"

"What exactly are you suggesting, Dr. Taub? That my son shouldn't compete because he's not from the right family? Because he doesn't have the right connections?"

"I think you're misunderstanding—"

"I understand perfectly." Grace's voice was steady now. Clear. "You're saying my son shouldn't compete because he's working class. Because his mother's a waitress and his father died in an accident. Because he doesn't have advantages."

Dr. Taub's face reddened. He looked around the restaurant. Other customers were listening. No one came to his rescue.

"You've been coming here twenty-three years," Grace said. "You've watched me serve you coffee. Listened to your opinions about everything. But you've never once asked about my son's dreams. Never asked about his talent. Now that he's entering a competition that might give him a chance, you're suddenly concerned about 'realistic expectations.'"

"Grace, I was trying to be helpful—"

"You're not being helpful. You're being condescending. You're telling me my son shouldn't compete because if he loses to someone with his background, what does that say about the world you believe in? The one where success goes to people who can afford it?"

Dr. Patterson looked at his coffee cup. "I think we should end this conversation—"

"We're done." Grace straightened her uniform. "Enjoy your pie, Dr. Patterson. It's made from apples grown in this town, served by people who live in this town. Maybe think about that next time you discuss what's realistic."

She walked to the next table—booth seven, young couple sharing dessert—and asked if they needed anything else. Her voice back to professional courtesy. As if nothing had happened. As if she hadn't just demolished the polite fiction that allowed Friendly's to function as neutral territory.

---

The manager, Tom Andrews, called her into the back room twenty minutes later. Fifteen years managing Friendly's, never seen anything like it. He had the conversation managers have with employees who violate the cardinal rule: never make customers uncomfortable with your humanity.

But Tom had grown up in Sudbury. Had worked construction with Dan Johnson. Had been to the funeral. Had watched Grace carry herself through circumstances that would have broken most people.

He gave her a lecture about professionalism and customer relations.

Then he gave her a raise.

Fifteen cents an hour.

Grace didn't know whether to laugh or cry. Fifteen cents for finally saying what everyone knew but pretended they didn't. For proving the help had opinions, feelings, children whose futures mattered.

---

The story spread through Sudbury by Monday morning. Everyone had heard some version of what happened at Friendly's. Details varied depending on who told it and what they needed it to mean.

Some said Grace had been rude to a customer. Some said Dr. Patterson had been condescending to a waitress. Some said it was a misunderstanding. Some said it was about time someone stood up to the attitude that made working-class people feel like they didn't belong in their own town.

Nick heard about it at school. Three different people told him his mom had "gone off" on a customer. He drove straight to Friendly's after practice, found Grace wiping down tables at the end of her shift.

"Mom. I heard—"

"It's fine, Nick."

"Did you really tell off Dr. Patterson?"

Grace looked at her son. Seventeen years old, guitar calluses on his fingers, Dan's eyes. "I told him the truth."

"What truth?"

"That you deserve a chance. Same as anyone."

Nick was quiet for a moment. Then: "You didn't have to do that."

"Yes," Grace said. "I did."

She finished wiping the table. Folded the rag. Untied her apron.

"Come on," she said. "Let's go home."

They walked out together into the parking lot. The Battle of the Bands was eight days away.

---
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 20: TEACHERS WHO FANNED THE FLAMES
**Third Person - May 5, 1979**
**Word Count Target:** 1,500 words

---

Bob Wentworth had been thinking about the photograph in his desk drawer. Nick and Jackie at twelve, arms around each other, holding guitars, smiling. The 1975 talent show. Before everything went wrong.

Tuesday afternoon jazz band rehearsal, two days before the Battle. Seventeen students warming up, the usual chaos of tuning and conversation. Nick on guitar near the window. Jackie at the piano across the room. They hadn't spoken in months.

"I want to try something different today," Wentworth said. He held up sheet music. "Dave Brubeck, 'Take Five.' It's in 5/4 time—off-balance, unexpected. Nick, Jackie, I want you two to work on this together. See if you can reimagine it."

The room went silent.

Nick looked at Jackie across the room. Two years of careful distance between them now.

"Mr. Wentworth," Nick said carefully. "I'm not sure this is a good idea."

"Sometimes the best way forward is to remember where you started."

Jackie was already moving to the piano. "I'll take the bass line." His voice steady, professional. Nothing like the kid he'd been at thirteen.

---

They started to play.

Jackie's left hand found Brubeck's unusual rhythm easily—classical training made the 5/4 time signature second nature. His right hand began adding flourishes, runs that transformed jazz sophistication into something more theatrical. Pure Freddie Mercury.

Nick listened. Found the spaces between Jackie's notes. Started threading blues-rock through the jazz structure. His guitar work tentative at first, testing the ice.

For thirty seconds, it worked.

Jackie's piano breathing. Nick's guitar answering. The rhythm off-balance but finding its center. Like two people remembering a conversation in a language they used to speak fluently.

Jackie added a crescendo. Nick matched it. The room disappeared. Just the music, the space between notes, the ghost of what they'd been.

Seventeen teenagers held their breath.

---

Then Don Gould walked in.

"Sounds like democracy in action!" His voice loud enough to shatter glass. "The American experiment in real time."

Nick's fingers stumbled. Jackie's right hand fell silent. Only the bass line continuing, suddenly lonely.

Gould taught AP American History, wore jeans on Fridays, encouraged students to call him "Don." He believed everything was a teachable moment.

"You know what this reminds me of?" Gould said. "The Lincoln-Douglas debates. Same fundamental tension, different century. Johnson here represents the Jacksonian tradition—man of the people, authentic democracy, rough edges and all. Marsh embodies the Jeffersonian ideal—educated, refined, excellence elevating everyone. Both American traditions!"

Nick stopped playing completely.

"We're just playing music," he said. His voice carrying an edge now.

"Are you though?" Gould smiled, warming to his theme. "Or are you playing out the eternal American tension between populism and intellectualism—"

"Between the kids who matter and the kids who don't?" Nick stood up so quickly his guitar strap caught on the music stand. Sheet music scattered across the floor. "Between the ones whose parents donate new instruments and the ones whose parents die in accidents that get blamed on worker error?"

Gould's face showed confusion. He'd thought he was facilitating dialogue.

"You want to make us a lesson?" Nick unplugged his guitar, movements precise and furious. "Fine. Here's your lesson. Jackie's going to Juilliard or Yale or wherever. I'm going to work construction like my dad. Maybe die quick like him too. That American enough?"

"Nick," Jackie said quietly. The first time he'd said Nick's name in two years.

"What?" Nick turned to face him. All the careful distance dissolving. "You want to pretend this is about music? Like we're equals because we can both play some notes?"

"That's not what I—"

"Your dad made it pretty clear. These boys don't understand boundaries."

Jackie's face changed. "That's not fair."

"No? Then why'd you move? Why'd you step aside like a good little prince letting the peasants pass?"

"Because I was trying to avoid this!" Jackie gestured at the space between them. "Because I thought maybe we could get through one week without—"

"Without what? Without admitting that Hop Brook might as well be the Atlantic Ocean? Without pretending your Queen covers aren't you slumming with real people?"

"Slumming?" Jackie's voice cracked. Suddenly he wasn't the professor's son or the classical prodigy. Just seventeen and tired of being blamed for advantages he'd never asked for. "You think this is slumming? You think I want—"

He stopped. Looked around the room. Their classmates watching. Their teachers judging.

"You know what? Forget it." Jackie's voice cold now. Controlled. "You want a war? Fine. Friday night, we'll see whose America wins."

He walked out. Didn't storm. Evacuated with dignity intact, the way his parents had taught him. The piano bench scraped against the floor.

---

Seventeen teenagers stared at Gould.

"I was just trying to provide historical context—"

"Don." Wentworth's voice carried exhaustion. "Get out."

---

May 7th, two days later. The hallways of Lincoln-Sudbury felt different. Nick and Jackie moved through the building like former friends who'd discovered they were enemies.

The Battle of the Bands was forty-one hours away.

Wentworth sat in his empty music room after school, looking at the photograph from 1975. Two boys, arms around each other, smiling. He'd tried to build a bridge with music. Gould had tried to build one with history lessons.

Both had failed.

You can't bridge a divide by explaining it. Can't heal a wound by describing its characteristics. Can't make harmony happen by pointing out it should be possible.

He put the photograph back in his drawer.

Friday night would answer the only question that mattered: what happens when it all comes crashing down?
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL
**Third Person - May 8, 1979 (Day Before the Battle)**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

The garage on Dutton Road still smelled like sawdust and motor oil. Dan Johnson's tools hung on the pegboard, organized with the precision of a man who'd made do with what he had. His work boots sat by the door, waiting.

Nick stood in the center of the space, surrounded by his father's memory and the weight of what tomorrow meant. Stephen Murphy, David Chen, and Mark Sullivan were there—the Lincoln boys, his band. Walking the Line. They'd been practicing for six hours.

"What if we're not good enough?" Mark asked during a break. His hands shaking as he adjusted his borrowed keyboard.

Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

The opening riff filled the garage. Raw. Powerful.

Stephen's bass locked in. David's drums provided the heartbeat. Mark's keyboard added texture. Together, they created something more than the sum of borrowed equipment and callused fingers.

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

The iconic bass line. Stephen locked into it perfectly, fingers finding the groove. They worked through the set: "Dream On," "Sweet Emotion," "Walk This Way," "Toys in the Attic."

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

"Walk This Way" was their closer. The song that gave everything its name. Simple guitar line building into something unstoppable.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.

"That's what we've got," Nick said.

---

Outside, Grace stood in the driveway, listening to her son's music drift through the walls.

She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping her at the grocery store now. Parents calling the house. Nick had become something bigger than just a teenager who liked to play guitar.

She leaned against the house, listening to four boys trying to figure out how to be a band, and wondered if she'd made the right choice when she'd stood up to Dr. Taub.

Nick was carrying something she wasn't sure he was ready for.

---

Inside, Nick practiced until the Lincoln boys finally went home, leaving him alone with Dan's tools and tomorrow's weight.

He sat on the workbench, guitar across his lap. The wood warm. The strings familiar.

This was where he'd learned to play. Where Dan had taught him the "Dream On" solo one Sunday afternoon, both of them hunched over the guitar, Dan's calloused hands guiding his until he got it right.

"You got the gift, Nicky," Dan had said. "Don't waste it."

Nick looked at his father's boots by the door. Three years since the accident. Three years of Grace working double shifts, of him practicing in this garage, of pretending music was just entertainment and not the only thing keeping him connected to a man who'd died eating a tuna sandwich at a construction site.

Tomorrow wasn't just about beating Jackie Marsh.

It was about proving that Dan hadn't been wrong. That the gift was real. That a $25 guitar and a garage full of borrowed equipment could make something that mattered.

Nick ran through "Dream On" one more time. Alone now. Just him and the ghost of his father's voice saying *you got the gift.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.

---
```

```plaintext
She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping her at the grocery store now. Parents calling the house. Nick had become something bigger than just a teenager who liked to play guitar.

She leaned against the house, listening to four boys trying to figure out how to be a band, and wondered if she'd made the right choice when she'd stood up to Dr. Taub.

Nick was carrying something she wasn't sure he was ready for.

---

Inside, Nick practiced until the Lincoln boys finally went home. He heard their car pull away, heard the silence settle.
```

```plaintext
Then the side door opened. Grace stood there, still in her Friendly's uniform.

"You should be asleep," Nick said.

"So should you." She came in, leaned against the workbench. "They sounded good. You all did."

"Mom—"

"Your father would be proud, you know."

Nick looked down at his guitar. "What if I'm not good enough?"

Grace was quiet for a moment. Outside, a car passed on Dutton Road. Inside, the garage smelled like sawdust and decades of Dan's work.

"You already are," she said. "You've been good enough since the day you picked up that guitar. Tomorrow's not about proving anything to anyone. It's about showing them what you already know."

She kissed the top of his head. "Don't stay up too late."

After she left, Nick sat on the workbench, guitar across his lap. The wood warm. The strings familiar.

This was where he'd learned to play. Where Dan had taught him the "Dream On" solo one Sunday afternoon, both of them hunched over the guitar, Dan's calloused hands guiding his until he got it right.

"You got the gift, Nicky," Dan had said. "Don't waste it."

Nick looked at his father's boots by the door. Three years since the accident. Three years of Grace working double shifts, of him practicing in this garage, of pretending music was just entertainment and not the only thing keeping him connected to a man who'd died eating a tuna sandwich at a construction site.

Tomorrow wasn't just about beating Jackie Marsh.
```

```plaintext
Nick knew what he was really afraid of. Not losing to Jackie. Not the town's disappointment. Not even proving Dr. Taub right about "realistic expectations."

He was afraid of looking at his mother's face after the Battle and seeing the same look she'd had at Dan's funeral. That quiet resignation. The look that said *we tried, we hoped, we lost.*

Grace had stood up at that PTA meeting. She'd confronted Dr. Taub at Friendly's. She'd put herself on the line for him. For his dream. For the idea that talent and hard work could matter more than money and connections.

What if she was wrong? What if tomorrow proved that the world worked exactly the way Dr. Taub said it did?

Nick ran his thumb across the guitar strings. They hummed in the silence.

Tomorrow wasn't about proving that Dan hadn't been wrong about the gift. It was about proving that Grace wasn't wrong to believe in it.

Nick ran through "Dream On" one more time. Alone now. Just him and the ghost of his father's voice saying *you got the gift.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.

---

**END CHAPTER 21**
```

```plaintext
Nick stood in the center of the space, surrounded by his father's memory and the weight of what tomorrow meant. Stephen Murphy, David Cassel, and Mark Pianka were there—the Lincoln boys, his band. Walking the Line. They'd been practicing for six hours.

"What if we're not good enough?" Mark asked during a break, adjusting his borrowed keyboard.

Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

The opening riff filled the garage. Raw. Powerful.

Stephen's bass locked in. David's ((wrong name)) drums provided the heartbeat. Mark's ((wrong name)) keyboard added texture. Together, they created something more than the sum of borrowed equipment and callused fingers.

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

The iconic bass line. Stephen locked into it perfectly, fingers finding the groove. They worked through the set: "Dream On," "Sweet Emotion," "Walk This Way," "Toys in the Attic."

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

"Walk This Way" was their closer. The song that gave everything its name. Simple guitar line building into something unstoppable.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.

"That's what we've got," Nick said.

Stephen set down his bass. "Nick. Whatever happens tomorrow—we're with you. Not because of your mom's speech or the town or any of that shit. Because you're the reason we started playing in the first place." ((great line!!))

Mark ((wrong name)) nodded. "Freshman year, you were the only kid who didn't laugh when I showed up with my grandmother's old Casio. You said, 'Can you play it?' Not 'Is that a real keyboard?'"((Amazing line))

David ((wrong name)) twirled a drumstick. "You taught me how to hold the sticks properly. Spent three lunches in a row just showing me the grip. You didn't have to do that."

"We're not here because you're carrying some working-class flag," Stephen said. "We're here because you made us believe we could actually be a band. So tomorrow? We play for that. Screw everything else." ((this new dialogue is PERFECT, I am almost crying it's so true and real and we need more of this))

Nick looked at the three of them. The Lincoln boys. His brothers in borrowed equipment and callused hands. "Let's run it one more time."

They did.

---

Outside, Grace stood in the driveway, listening to her son's music drift through the walls.

She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping her at the grocery store now. Parents calling the house. Nick had become something bigger than just a teenager who liked to play guitar. ((Good, bordering on not belieavable that Nick has become like a rock star in his own town as we describe here.  Desctiption is good but maybe tone it down ... use your words ... but it could be something like, "Grace was suprised at how many people in town knew about the Battle of the Bands, knew about this guitar on the rise ... "))

She leaned against the house, listening to four boys trying to figure out how to be a band, and wondered if she'd made the right choice when she'd stood up to Dr. Taub.

Nick was carrying something she wasn't sure he was ready for. ((I like the line here, but not sure exactly what it means, please explain))

---

Inside, Nick practiced until the Lincoln boys finally went home. He heard their car pull away, heard the silence settle.

Then the side door opened. Grace stood there, still in her Friendly's uniform.

"You should be asleep," Nick said.

"So should you." She came in, leaned against the workbench. "They sounded good (("good" might not be the right word here maybe a better descrition of the music from Grace to give her more depth)). You all did."

"Mom—"

"Your father would be proud, you know."

Nick looked down at his guitar. "What if I'm not good enough?"

Grace was quiet for a moment. Outside, a car passed on Dutton Road. Inside, the garage smelled like sawdust ((we have used this "Sawdust" term numerous times please scan the novel and see how many times we use it.  This is a good opportunity to have one of those desciptions like brown grass poking through the snow like a dead man's stubble ... something strong like that we need more prose like that))and decades of Dan's work.

"You already are," she said. "You've been good enough since the day you picked up that guitar. Tomorrow's not about proving anything to anyone. It's about showing them what you already know."

She kissed the top of his head. "Don't stay up too late."

After she left, Nick sat on the workbench, guitar across his lap. The wood warm. The strings familiar.

This was where he'd learned to play. Where Dan had taught him the "Dream On" solo one Sunday afternoon, both of them hunched over the guitar, Dan's calloused hands guiding his until he got it right.

"You got the gift, Nicky," Dan had said. "Don't waste it."

Nick looked at his father's boots by the door ((need something else as this is not believable to me )). Three years since the accident. Three years of Grace working double shifts, of him practicing in this garage, of pretending music was just entertainment and not the only thing keeping him connected to a man ((don't like the ending of this sentence as it seems out of place and inappropriate ))who'd died eating a tuna sandwich at a construction site.

Tomorrow wasn't just about beating Jackie Marsh.

Nick knew what he was really afraid of. Not losing to Jackie. Not the town's disappointment. Not even proving Dr. Taub right about "realistic expectations."

He was afraid of looking at his mother's face after the Battle and seeing the same look she'd had at Dan's funeral. That quiet resignation. ((maybe another way to write this would be something about not letting his mother down, not letting his family down, not letting himself down.  This battle was real and Nick wante this badly ... I don;t know something like this maybe?))The look that said *we tried, we hoped, we lost.*

Grace had stood up at that PTA meeting. She'd confronted Dr. Taub at Friendly's. She'd put herself on the line for him. For his dream. For the idea that talent and hard work could matter more than money and connections ((too much reliance on stating what should be obvious by the characters actions to this point in the story.  Grace put her herself on the the line for Nick and when he thought of this he felt a certain ping in his body that was hard to pinpoint or fully comprehend like a ...)).

What if she was wrong? What if tomorrow proved that the world worked exactly the way Dr. Taub said it did?  ((this is good!!  Not--restating issues that the readers already know about))

Nick ran his thumb across the guitar strings. They hummed in the silence.((i love this jsut check if we have used the exact description before as it sounds familar like we used it previously))

Tomorrow wasn't about proving that Dan hadn't been wrong about the gift. It was about proving that Grace wasn't wrong to believe in it. ((a little wordy here ... but this sentence is CRITICAL ... this is one of the things that drives Nick & readers want to understand the deeper insides of Nick and the main charactoers))

Nick ran through "Dream On" one more time. Alone now. Just him and the ghost of his father's voice saying *you got the gift.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL
**Third Person - May 8, 1979 (Day Before the Battle)**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

The garage on Dutton Road smelled like old concrete and machine grease—the kind that soaks into floors and never leaves. Dan Johnson's tools hung on the pegboard, organized with the precision of a man who'd made do with what he had. His old Craftsman toolbox sat in the corner, latches rusted shut, exactly where he'd left it three years ago.

Nick stood in the center of the space, surrounded by his father's memory and the weight of what tomorrow meant. Stephen Murphy, David Cassel, and Mark Pianka were there—the Lincoln boys, his band. Walking the Line. They'd been practicing for six hours.

"What if we're not good enough?" Mark asked during a break, adjusting his borrowed keyboard.

Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

The opening riff filled the garage. Raw. Powerful.

Stephen's bass locked in. David's drums provided the heartbeat. Mark's keyboard added texture. Together, they created something more than the sum of borrowed equipment and callused fingers.

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

The iconic bass line. Stephen locked into it perfectly, fingers finding the groove. They worked through the set: "Dream On," "Sweet Emotion," "Walk This Way," "Toys in the Attic."

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

"Walk This Way" was their closer. The song that gave everything its name. Simple guitar line building into something unstoppable.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.

"That's what we've got," Nick said.

Stephen set down his bass. "Nick. Whatever happens tomorrow—we're with you. Not because of your mom's speech or the town or any of that shit. Because you're the reason we started playing in the first place."
```

```plaintext
Mark nodded. "Freshman year, you were the only kid who didn't laugh when I showed up with my grandmother's old Casio. You said, 'Can you play it?' Not 'Is that a real keyboard?'"

David twirled a drumstick. "You taught me how to hold the sticks properly. Spent three lunches in a row just showing me the grip. You didn't have to do that."

"We're not here because you're carrying some working-class flag," Stephen said. "We're here because you made us believe we could actually be a band. So tomorrow? We play for that. Screw everything else."

Nick looked at the three of them. The Lincoln boys. His brothers in borrowed equipment and callused hands. "Let's run it one more time."

They did.

---

Outside, Grace stood in the driveway, listening to her son's music drift through the walls.

She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping her at the grocery store now. Parents calling the house. Nick had become something bigger than just a teenager who liked to play guitar. ((Good, bordering on not belieavable that Nick has become like a rock star in his own town as we describe here.  Desctiption is good but maybe tone it down ... use your words ... but it could be something like, "Grace was suprised at how many people in town knew about the Battle of the Bands, knew about this guitar on the rise ... "))

She leaned against the house, listening to four boys trying to figure out how to be a band, and wondered if she'd made the right choice when she'd stood up to Dr. Taub.

Nick was carrying something she wasn't sure he was ready for. ((I like the line here, but not sure exactly what it means, please explain))

---

Inside, Nick practiced until the Lincoln boys finally went home. He heard their car pull away, heard the silence settle.

Then the side door opened. Grace stood there, still in her Friendly's uniform.

"You should be asleep," Nick said.

"So should you." She came in, leaned against the workbench. "They sounded good (("good" might not be the right word here maybe a better descrition of the music from Grace to give her more depth)). You all did."

"Mom—"

"Your father would be proud, you know."

Nick looked down at his guitar. "What if I'm not good enough?"

Grace was quiet for a moment. Outside, a car passed on Dutton Road. Inside, the garage smelled like sawdust ((we have used this "Sawdust" term numerous times please scan the novel and see how many times we use it.  This is a good opportunity to have one of those desciptions like brown grass poking through the snow like a dead man's stubble ... something strong like that we need more prose like that))and decades of Dan's work.

"You already are," she said. "You've been good enough since the day you picked up that guitar. Tomorrow's not about proving anything to anyone. It's about showing them what you already know."

She kissed the top of his head. "Don't stay up too late."

After she left, Nick sat on the workbench, guitar across his lap. The wood warm. The strings familiar.

This was where he'd learned to play. Where Dan had taught him the "Dream On" solo one Sunday afternoon, both of them hunched over the guitar, Dan's calloused hands guiding his until he got it right.

"You got the gift, Nicky," Dan had said. "Don't waste it."

Nick looked at his father's boots by the door ((need something else as this is not believable to me )). Three years since the accident. Three years of Grace working double shifts, of him practicing in this garage, of pretending music was just entertainment and not the only thing keeping him connected to a man ((don't like the ending of this sentence as it seems out of place and inappropriate ))who'd died eating a tuna sandwich at a construction site.

Tomorrow wasn't just about beating Jackie Marsh.

Nick knew what he was really afraid of. Not losing to Jackie. Not the town's disappointment. Not even proving Dr. Taub right about "realistic expectations."

He was afraid of looking at his mother's face after the Battle and seeing the same look she'd had at Dan's funeral. That quiet resignation. ((maybe another way to write this would be something about not letting his mother down, not letting his family down, not letting himself down.  This battle was real and Nick wante this badly ... I don;t know something like this maybe?))The look that said *we tried, we hoped, we lost.*

Grace had stood up at that PTA meeting. She'd confronted Dr. Taub at Friendly's. She'd put herself on the line for him. For his dream. For the idea that talent and hard work could matter more than money and connections ((too much reliance on stating what should be obvious by the characters actions to this point in the story.  Grace put her herself on the the line for Nick and when he thought of this he felt a certain ping in his body that was hard to pinpoint or fully comprehend like a ...)).

What if she was wrong? What if tomorrow proved that the world worked exactly the way Dr. Taub said it did?  ((this is good!!  Not--restating issues that the readers already know about))

Nick ran his thumb across the guitar strings. They hummed in the silence.((i love this jsut check if we have used the exact description before as it sounds familar like we used it previously))

Tomorrow wasn't about proving that Dan hadn't been wrong about the gift. It was about proving that Grace wasn't wrong to believe in it. ((a little wordy here ... but this sentence is CRITICAL ... this is one of the things that drives Nick & readers want to understand the deeper insides of Nick and the main charactoers))

Nick ran through "Dream On" one more time. Alone now. Just him and the ghost of his father's voice saying *you got the gift.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL
**Third Person - May 8, 1979 (Day Before the Battle)**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

The garage on Dutton Road smelled like old concrete and machine grease—the kind that soaks into floors and never leaves. Dan Johnson's tools hung on the pegboard, organized with the precision of a man who'd made do with what he had. His old Craftsman toolbox sat in the corner, latches rusted shut, exactly where he'd left it three years ago.

Nick stood in the center of the space, surrounded by his father's memory and the weight of what tomorrow meant. Stephen Murphy, David Cassel, and Mark Pianka were there—the Lincoln boys, his band. Walking the Line. They'd been practicing for six hours.

"What if we're not good enough?" Mark asked during a break, adjusting his borrowed keyboard.

Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

The opening riff filled the garage. Raw. Powerful.

Stephen's bass locked in. David's drums provided the heartbeat. Mark's keyboard added texture. Together, they created something more than the sum of borrowed equipment and callused fingers.

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

The iconic bass line. Stephen locked into it perfectly, fingers finding the groove. They worked through the set: "Dream On," "Sweet Emotion," "Walk This Way," "Toys in the Attic."

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

"Walk This Way" was their closer. The song that gave everything its name. Simple guitar line building into something unstoppable.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.

"That's what we've got," Nick said.

Stephen set down his bass. "Nick. Whatever happens tomorrow—we're with you. Not because of your mom's speech or the town or any of that shit. Because you're the reason we started playing in the first place."

Mark nodded. "Freshman year, you were the only kid who didn't laugh when I showed up with my grandmother's old Casio. You said, 'Can you play it?' Not 'Is that a real keyboard?'"

David twirled a drumstick. "You taught me how to hold the sticks properly. Spent three lunches in a row just showing me the grip. You didn't have to do that."

"We're not here because you're carrying some working-class flag," Stephen said. "We're here because you made us believe we could actually be a band. So tomorrow? We play for that. Screw everything else."

Nick looked at the three of them. The Lincoln boys. His brothers in borrowed equipment and callused hands. "Let's run it one more time."

They did.

---

Outside, Grace stood in the driveway, listening to her son's music drift through the garage walls.

She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's had turned into something she hadn't anticipated. She was surprised how many people in town had heard about the Battle of the Bands, how many knew about Nick, how many had opinions about which way it should go.
```

```plaintext
But what surprised her more was how much Nick had changed since Dan died.

The guitar had started as grief management—a way for a fourteen-year-old boy to stay connected to his father. Grace had encouraged it. What else could she do? She couldn't bring Dan back. She couldn't fix what the accident had broken. But she could let Nick play.

Except somewhere along the way, the playing had become something else. An obsession. A mission. The garage wasn't just where Nick practiced anymore—it was where he disappeared for hours, chasing something she couldn't see, reaching for something she couldn't name.

She was afraid of what would happen if he lost tomorrow. Would it destroy him the way Dan's death had almost destroyed her? Would he see it as proof that the gift Dan had seen wasn't real?

But she was also afraid of what would happen if he won. Would music take him away from her too? Would he chase that dream until it killed him, just like construction had killed Dan?

Grace leaned against the house, listening to four boys trying to figure out how to be a band, and pushed those thoughts down. She'd made her choice when she'd stood up to Dr. Taub. Now she had to live with it.

---

Inside, Nick practiced until the Lincoln boys finally went home. He heard their car pull away, heard the silence settle.

Then the side door opened. Grace stood there, still in her Friendly's uniform.

"You should be asleep," Nick said.

"So should you." She came in, leaned against the workbench. "It sounded like your father was in here with you. All of you."

"Mom—"

"Your father would be proud, you know."

Nick looked down at his guitar. "What if I'm not good enough?"

Grace was quiet for a moment. Outside, a car passed on Dutton Road. Inside, the garage smelled like machine oil and memory—the kind that gets into your clothes and won't wash out, no matter how many times you try.

"You already are," she said. "You've been good enough since the day you picked up that guitar. Tomorrow's not about proving anything to anyone. It's about showing them what you already know."

She kissed the top of his head. "Don't stay up too late."

After she left, Nick sat on the workbench, guitar across his lap. The wood warm. The strings familiar.

This was where he'd learned to play. Where Dan had taught him the "Dream On" solo one Sunday afternoon, both of them hunched over the guitar, Dan's calloused hands guiding his until he got it right.

"You got the gift, Nicky," Dan had said. "Don't waste it."

Nick looked at his father's boots by the door ((need something else as this is not believable to me )). Three years since the accident. Three years of Grace working double shifts, of him practicing in this garage, of pretending music was just entertainment and not the only thing keeping him connected to a man ((don't like the ending of this sentence as it seems out of place and inappropriate ))who'd died eating a tuna sandwich at a construction site.

Tomorrow wasn't just about beating Jackie Marsh.

Nick knew what he was really afraid of. Not losing to Jackie. Not the town's disappointment. Not even proving Dr. Taub right about "realistic expectations."

He was afraid of looking at his mother's face after the Battle and seeing the same look she'd had at Dan's funeral. That quiet resignation. ((maybe another way to write this would be something about not letting his mother down, not letting his family down, not letting himself down.  This battle was real and Nick wante this badly ... I don;t know something like this maybe?))The look that said *we tried, we hoped, we lost.*

Grace had stood up at that PTA meeting. She'd confronted Dr. Taub at Friendly's. She'd put herself on the line for him. For his dream. For the idea that talent and hard work could matter more than money and connections ((too much reliance on stating what should be obvious by the characters actions to this point in the story.  Grace put her herself on the the line for Nick and when he thought of this he felt a certain ping in his body that was hard to pinpoint or fully comprehend like a ...)).

What if she was wrong? What if tomorrow proved that the world worked exactly the way Dr. Taub said it did?  ((this is good!!  Not--restating issues that the readers already know about))

Nick ran his thumb across the guitar strings. They hummed in the silence.((i love this jsut check if we have used the exact description before as it sounds familar like we used it previously))

Tomorrow wasn't about proving that Dan hadn't been wrong about the gift. It was about proving that Grace wasn't wrong to believe in it. ((a little wordy here ... but this sentence is CRITICAL ... this is one of the things that drives Nick & readers want to understand the deeper insides of Nick and the main charactoers))

Nick ran through "Dream On" one more time. Alone now. Just him and the ghost of his father's voice saying *you got the gift.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.

---

**END CHAPTER 21**
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL
**Third Person - May 8, 1979 (Day Before the Battle)**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

The garage on Dutton Road smelled like old concrete and machine grease—the kind that soaks into floors and never leaves. Dan Johnson's tools hung on the pegboard, organized with the precision of a man who'd made do with what he had. His old Craftsman toolbox sat in the corner, latches rusted shut, exactly where he'd left it three years ago.

Nick stood in the center of the space, surrounded by his father's memory and the weight of what tomorrow meant. Stephen Murphy, David Cassel, and Mark Pianka were there—the Lincoln boys, his band. Walking the Line. They'd been practicing for six hours.

"What if we're not good enough?" Mark asked during a break, adjusting his borrowed keyboard.

Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

The opening riff filled the garage. Raw. Powerful.

Stephen's bass locked in. David's drums provided the heartbeat. Mark's keyboard added texture. Together, they created something more than the sum of borrowed equipment and callused fingers.

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

The iconic bass line. Stephen locked into it perfectly, fingers finding the groove. They worked through the set: "Dream On," "Sweet Emotion," "Walk This Way," "Toys in the Attic."

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

"Walk This Way" was their closer. The song that gave everything its name. Simple guitar line building into something unstoppable.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.

"That's what we've got," Nick said.

Stephen set down his bass. "Nick. Whatever happens tomorrow—we're with you. Not because of your mom's speech or the town or any of that shit. Because you're the reason we started playing in the first place."

Mark nodded. "Freshman year, you were the only kid who didn't laugh when I showed up with my grandmother's old Casio. You said, 'Can you play it?' Not 'Is that a real keyboard?'"

David twirled a drumstick. "You taught me how to hold the sticks properly. Spent three lunches in a row just showing me the grip. You didn't have to do that."

"We're not here because you're carrying some working-class flag," Stephen said. "We're here because you made us believe we could actually be a band. So tomorrow? We play for that. Screw everything else."

Nick looked at the three of them. The Lincoln boys. His brothers in borrowed equipment and callused hands. "Let's run it one more time."

They did.

---

Outside, Grace stood in the driveway, listening to her son's music drift through the garage walls.

She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's had turned into something she hadn't anticipated. She was surprised how many people in town had heard about the Battle of the Bands, how many knew about Nick, how many had opinions about which way it should go.

But what surprised her more was how much Nick had changed since Dan died.

The guitar had started as grief management—a way for a fourteen-year-old boy to stay connected to his father. Grace had encouraged it. What else could she do? She couldn't bring Dan back. She couldn't fix what the accident had broken. But she could let Nick play.

Except somewhere along the way, the playing had become something else. An obsession. A mission. The garage wasn't just where Nick practiced anymore—it was where he disappeared for hours, chasing something she couldn't see, reaching for something she couldn't name.

She was afraid of what would happen if he lost tomorrow. Would it destroy him the way Dan's death had almost destroyed her? Would he see it as proof that the gift Dan had seen wasn't real?

But she was also afraid of what would happen if he won. Would music take him away from her too? Would he chase that dream until it killed him, just like construction had killed Dan?

Grace leaned against the house, listening to four boys trying to figure out how to be a band, and pushed those thoughts down. She'd made her choice when she'd stood up to Dr. Taub. Now she had to live with it.

---

Inside, Nick practiced until the Lincoln boys finally went home. He heard their car pull away, heard the silence settle.

Then the side door opened. Grace stood there, still in her Friendly's uniform.

"You should be asleep," Nick said.

"So should you." She came in, leaned against the workbench. "It sounded like your father was in here with you. All of you."

"Mom—"

"Your father would be proud, you know."

Nick looked down at his guitar. "What if I'm not good enough?"

Grace was quiet for a moment. Outside, a car passed on Dutton Road. Inside, the garage smelled like machine oil and memory—the kind that gets into your clothes and won't wash out, no matter how many times you try.

"You already are," she said. "You've been good enough since the day you picked up that guitar. Tomorrow's not about proving anything to anyone. It's about showing them what you already know."

She kissed the top of his head. "Don't stay up too late."

After she left, Nick sat on the workbench, guitar across his lap. The wood warm. The strings familiar.

This was where he'd learned to play. Where Dan had taught him the "Dream On" solo one Sunday afternoon, both of them hunched over the guitar, Dan's calloused hands guiding his until he got it right.

"You got the gift, Nicky," Dan had said. "Don't waste it."

Nick looked at the Craftsman toolbox in the corner, latches rusted shut. Three years and Grace still couldn't bring herself to open it. Three years of her working double shifts. Three years of him in this garage, pretending the guitar was just a hobby and not the last thread connecting him to his father.

Tomorrow wasn't just about beating Jackie Marsh.

Nick knew what he was really afraid of. Not losing to Jackie. Not the town's disappointment. Not even proving Dr. Taub right about "realistic expectations."

He was afraid of letting her down. Of proving that every risk she'd taken—standing up at that PTA meeting, confronting Dr. Taub at Friendly's, putting herself on the line—had been for nothing.

When he thought about it, he felt something tighten in his chest. Not quite panic. Not quite dread. Something heavier, like carrying a weight you can't put down but aren't sure you can hold.

What if she was wrong? What if tomorrow proved that the world worked exactly the way Dr. Taub said it did?

Nick pressed his palm against the guitar's body, feeling the wood vibrate under his hand.

He wasn't playing for Dan's memory anymore. He was playing for the woman who'd stood up to the world and said her son mattered.

Nick ran through "Dream On" one more time. Alone now. Just him and the ghost of his father's voice saying *you got the gift.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.

---

**END CHAPTER 21**

**Word Count:** ~700 words

---
```

```plaintext
Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL
**Third Person - May 8, 1979 (Day Before the Battle)**
**Word Count Target:** 1,200-1,500 words

---

The garage on Dutton Road smelled like old concrete and machine grease—the kind that soaks into floors and never leaves. Dan Johnson's tools hung on the pegboard, organized with the precision of a man who'd made do with what he had.

Nick stood in the center of the space, surrounded by his father's memory and the weight of what tomorrow meant. Stephen Murphy, David Cassel, and Mark Pianka were there—the Lincoln boys, his band. Walking the Line. They'd been practicing for four hours straight.

"What if we're not good enough?" Mark asked during a break, adjusting his borrowed keyboard.

Nick picked up his guitar. The $25 acoustic Dan had bought him three years ago, worn smooth by practice. "We are."

"But what if we lose?" Stephen pressed.

Nick didn't answer. He'd been asking himself the same question every night since his mother's speech at Friendly's. Kids stopping him in hallways, telling him they were rooting for him. Parents asking Grace how he was doing. Like he was carrying something bigger than his own dreams.

And maybe he was.

"Let's run 'Dream On' again," Nick said.

---

The opening riff filled the garage. Raw. Powerful.

Stephen's bass locked in. David's drums provided the heartbeat. Mark's keyboard added texture. Together, they created something more than the sum of borrowed equipment and work-worn hands.

Nick had always loved "Dream On." The way it built from quiet desperation to full-throated defiance. Tyler's raw vocals speaking to something deep he couldn't name.

But tonight it felt different. Heavier.

When they finished, Stephen nodded. "That's the best we've ever played it."

"'Sweet Emotion,'" Nick said.

The iconic bass line. Stephen locked into it perfectly, fingers finding the groove. They worked through the set: "Dream On," "Sweet Emotion," "Walk This Way," "Toys in the Attic."

Each song carrying weight now. Not just notes and chords.

"Walk This Way" was their closer. The song that gave everything its name. Simple guitar line building into something unstoppable.

When they finished, the garage was silent except for breathing.

"That's what we've got," Nick said.

Stephen set down his bass. "Nick. Whatever happens tomorrow—we're with you. Not because of your mom's speech or the town or any of that shit. Because you're the reason we started playing in the first place."

Mark nodded. "Freshman year, you were the only kid who didn't laugh when I showed up with my grandmother's old Casio. You said, 'Can you play it?' Not 'Is that a real keyboard?'"

David twirled a drumstick. "You taught me how to hold the sticks properly. Spent three lunches in a row just showing me the grip. You didn't have to do that."

"We're not here because you're carrying some working-class flag," Stephen said. "We're here because you made us believe we could actually be a band. So tomorrow? We play for that. Screw everything else."

Nick looked at the three of them. The Lincoln boys. His brothers in borrowed equipment and split-knuckled determination. "Let's run it one more time."

They did.

---

Outside, Grace stood in the driveway, listening to her son's music drift through the garage walls.

She'd never meant for it to happen this way. The speech at Friendly's had turned into something she hadn't anticipated. She was surprised how many people in town had heard about the Battle of the Bands, how many knew about Nick, how many had opinions about which way it should go.

But what surprised her more was how much Nick had changed since Dan died.
```

```plaintext
Dan had taught Nick the guitar—that had been their bond, that connection words couldn't describe. But after the accident, the playing had become something else entirely. Grace had encouraged it. What else could she do? She couldn't bring Dan back. She couldn't fix what was broken. But she could let Nick play.

Except somewhere along the way, the playing had become something else. An obsession. A mission. The garage wasn't just where Nick practiced anymore—it was where he disappeared for hours, chasing something she couldn't see, reaching for something she couldn't name.

She was afraid of what would happen if he lost tomorrow. Would it destroy him the way Dan's death had almost destroyed her? Would he see it as proof that the gift Dan had seen wasn't real?
```
