```plaintext
What I don't tell the listeners: I thought I could fix it. 

That was my hubris. Forty years spinning records for bands nobody else 
would touch, and I'd started to believe I was the savior. Aerosmith, 
The Cars, Boston—I'd played them when they were nobody. They became 
somebody. I did that.

But Nick and Jackie? I couldn't save them. First time I failed. First 
time I realized I wasn't choosing the winners—I was just documenting the 
casualties.

And now, sitting here in Studio B for the last time, watching fifty-six 
years of rock radio get erased by corporate consolidation, I finally see 
the parallel. The station is Nick and Jackie. The same forces that divided 
those boys are shutting off our transmitter.

Same labyrinth. Different decade. Same ending.

Tomorrow, WBCN goes dark. Just like their friendship. Just like every 
real thing that dared to exist without permission from people who count 
money instead of listening to music.

But I have one last act of rebellion. One last choice that's actually 
mine. The demo tape. The forbidden recording. The proof that harmony 
existed before the world killed it.

Tonight, I'm going to play it. And if they sue me? Good. Let them try 
to silence a dead station.
```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 23: MAXANNE - THE EVE OF BATTLE

---

Six hours into the broadcast. Two hours left.

Studio B smells like fifty years of cigarette smoke that never quite left the walls, even after they banned smoking in 1995. The ON AIR light glows red above the door. Outside the booth, the station is empty—everyone evacuated hours ago, desks cleared, computers dark, forty-four years of rock radio reduced to boxes in a hallway waiting for someone to decide what gets saved and what gets thrown away.

I reach for the bourbon. Tyler sent me this bottle in 1976, after "Dream On" went gold. He sent one every Christmas until 1980, then stopped. This is the last one. I've been saving it for forty-eight years. Tonight seems like the right night to finish it.

The glass is half-empty now. My hands are steady. That's the thing about guilt—you carry it long enough, it stops shaking you. It just sits there, heavy and permanent, like scar tissue around your heart.

I cue "Bohemian Rhapsody." The full six minutes, no radio edit. Because tonight we have time. Tomorrow we have nothing.

---

The Battle of the Bands was my idea.

Not mine alone—Tom Andrews and I pitched it together in the fall of 1978. Regional high school competition, WBCN sponsorship, prize money and a recording session for the winners. We sold it to management as a marketing campaign: discover the next Aerosmith before they need us, drive listeners in the 15-25 demographic, attract sponsors who wanted access to that audience.

It made sense. Corporate consolidation was already starting—you could feel it coming like weather, the way playlists were tightening, the way management kept talking about "target demographics" instead of just playing music that mattered. The station needed money to stay independent. Content that drives listeners equals power to stay rebel. I thought I could game the system. Use capitalism to fund rebellion.

I'd discovered Aerosmith in 1973. Broke The Cars when they were still playing dive bars in Cambridge. Gave Boston their first airtime when everyone else thought they were too polished. I had the track record. I had the ear. I thought I could make stars, control outcomes, find lightning and bottle it.

The Battle of the Bands was supposed to prove that. Marketing genius wrapped in artistic legitimacy. Find talent, give them a platform, turn a high school talent show into something that mattered.

I thought I was the architect of success.

Turns out I was the architect of tragedy.

---

March 15, 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium, 985 seats packed with people who'd chosen sides before the first note was played. I sat in the judge's panel between two other WBCN DJs, clipboard in hand, trying to look professional while watching something die in real time.

Nick Johnson's band—Walking the Line—four kids from the northeast neighborhoods with duct-taped equipment and more hunger than technical skill. They played "Walk This Way" like their lives depended on it, because maybe they did. I could see Grace Johnson in the third row, still wearing her Friendly's uniform, hands gripped together in her lap like she was praying.

Jackie Marsh's band—Crown Jewels—four kids with professional equipment and the kind of technical precision that comes from expensive lessons and parents who can afford to care about things beyond making rent. They played "Bohemian Rhapsody" flawlessly. Every note perfect. Every harmony arranged. Empty as a mansion with no one home.

The crowd wasn't cheering music. They were cheering class warfare made visible. Working-class kids roared for Nick. College-prep crowd applauded for Jackie. The cafeteria geography of Lincoln-Sudbury turned into tribal warfare, and I'd built the arena.

Nick and Jackie didn't look at each other. Not once. Not during setup, not during performances, not when the MC announced Walking the Line as winners and Nick stood on stage holding a trophy that felt like an accusation instead of an achievement.

I watched their friendship die in front of 985 witnesses. Public execution disguised as competition. And I'd sold the tickets.

---

Here's what I tell myself, on nights when the bourbon doesn't help: I didn't create their division.

High school did that. Hop Brook geography did that. Dan Johnson's death in November 1977 did that—grief builds walls faster than friendship can climb them. Dr. Marsh's pressure on Jackie did that. Class warfare did that. America did that.

Two boys who once harmonized so perfectly it made teachers cry had been drifting apart for years. The labyrinth was killing them slowly. Private tragedy, the kind that happens to friendships every day. They might have found their way back to each other eventually, or they might not have. That's how innocence dies—quietly, gradually, in the spaces between conversations that never happen.

But I took that slow, private death and turned it into public spectacle. I saw two boys drifting apart and said, "Let's make them fight on stage. For sponsors. For content. For money."

I didn't kill their friendship. But I gave class warfare a microphone. I sold tickets to watch innocence die. I turned tragedy into entertainment.

And then I called it opportunity.

---

I left WBCN in 1980. One year after the Battle. Exactly one year.

The official reason was career advancement. Danny Goldberg's management company offered me a job doing national tour promotion. More money, more influence, more power to shape careers from the industry side instead of the radio side. Record label A&R work, artist management, the kind of position that meant I'd made it.

I told everyone it was the logical next step. Seven years breaking bands on-air, now I'd help them from behind the scenes. Still in music, just a different angle. People congratulated me. Tom Andrews threw me a going-away party. Steven Tyler sent bourbon.

But here's what I knew, sitting in this booth on my last night in 1980, watching the sun come up over Boston:

I was fleeing.

Not from failure—from success. The Battle of the Bands had been successful. Great ratings, strong sponsorship, management wanted to make it annual. I'd proven I could turn content into money, tragedy into product.

And I couldn't face what I'd become.

Corporate consolidation was accelerating. I could see the future: playlists, safe choices, turning rebellion into brand identity, packaging authenticity for suburban consumption. WBCN would survive by compromising, gradually, until the rebel station became just another frequency selling nostalgia for what it used to be.

I left before I had to compromise. I thought that was the smart choice. I thought leaving meant I'd preserved something pure.

Forty-four years later, I can see the truth: Leaving was the compromise. I traded my voice for survival. I went corporate. I became what I fought. Just quietly. Just gradually. Just the same as if I'd stayed.

---

The song reaches the opera section. Freddie Mercury's voice soars through Studio B, filling the empty station with sound that cost someone everything to create. He died in 1991. AIDS, thirty years of medicine too late. Another casualty of a world that punishes people for being what they are.

I take another sip of bourbon. Tyler's gift, nearly half a century old, tastes like regret.

Forty-four years in corporate music. A&R, promotion, artist management. I helped bands get signed—the safe ones, the ones that fit the formula, the ones that wouldn't challenge anything. I survived by becoming the machinery.

I told myself I was still in music. Still helping artists. Still connected to what mattered.

But I wasn't on-air. I wasn't speaking. I'd gone silent.

The rebel DJ who turned the volume to full and didn't give a damn what anyone thought became a corporate suit who measured risk and calculated demographics and helped turn art into product.

I survived. Nick and Jackie didn't—their potential erased, their friendship killed, their music silenced. WBCN survived until 2024, compromising gradually until corporate consolidation killed it anyway.

Three casualties of the same war. Three different strategies. Same outcome.

Nick stayed real. The system crushed him.

Jackie compromised. The system crushed him.

I fled. The system followed me.

The labyrinth has no exit. Fight, compromise, or run—you die regardless. Just different timelines. Just different flavors of the same defeat.

---

"Bohemian Rhapsody" builds toward the rock section. "So you think you can stone me and spit in my eye..."

I know why the station brought me back. Not for nostalgia week. Not to "celebrate" forty-four years of rock radio before corporate overlords flip the switch.

They brought me back because I'm the mirror. The cautionary tale. The one who left in 1980 and went corporate and survived by becoming complicit.

Look what you became, the empty station says. You left. We stayed. We all died anyway. Now tell that story on your way out. Confession disguised as celebration.

I could have said no. I'd been silent for forty-four years. Why come back?

Because the station's death gives me permission. You can't fire someone from a corpse. You can't blacklist someone when the industry's already dead. This is my last chance to break forty-four years of silence. To tell the truth about what I did. What we all did.

Not redemption. I can't undo March 15, 1979. I can't bring back Nick and Jackie's friendship. I can't restore WBCN's rebel soul. I can't un-become what I became.

Just confession. Just witness. Just: This is what I did. This is what my ambition cost. This is what we lose when we turn children into content, friendship into competition, art into product.

The labyrinth wins. Always. That's not a question.

But someone has to say it out loud. Someone has to document what we kill. Someone has to refuse to let the machinery erase even the memory of what existed before we destroyed it.

That's all I have. It's not redemption. It's not hope. It's not even resistance.

It's just: I saw it. I participated. And before the lights go out, I'm telling you what we did.

---

The song ends. Six minutes of Freddie Mercury's genius, fading to silence in an empty station.

I lean into the microphone. The ON AIR light pulses like a heartbeat running out of time.

"May 9th, 1979," I say. "Twenty-four hours before the Battle of the Bands. My Battle. My idea. My destruction."

My voice is steady. Forty-four years of practice at not shaking.

"Two boys in different rooms. Nick Johnson in his garage on Dutton Road, surrounded by his dead father's tools. Jackie Marsh in his basement studio, surrounded by his father's expectations. Both carrying more weight than any seventeen-year-old should carry. Both making choices they didn't understand yet. Both heading toward a stage I built for them."

I reach for the next cart. "Dream On." Aerosmith. The band that made me believe I was magic.

"Neither of them knowing what I'd created. What I'd done to their friendship. What the labyrinth does to innocence. Every time. Forever."

I press play.

"This is 'Dream On.' The band I discovered in 1973. The band that proved I had the ear. The band that made me think I could control outcomes."

Steven Tyler's voice fills the booth. That opening piano, haunting and pure, from back when they were nobody and I gave them everything.

"Twenty-four hours before I learned I couldn't save anyone."

I sit back. The bourbon glass catches the red glow of the ON AIR light.

"Including myself."

---

**END CHAPTER 23**

**Word Count: 1,847**

```

```plaintext
CHAPTER 23: MAXANNE - THE EVE OF BATTLE

---

Three hours into the broadcast. One hour left.

Studio B smells like fifty years of cigarette smoke that never quite left the walls, even after they banned smoking in 1995. The ON AIR light glows red above the door. Outside the booth, the station is empty—everyone evacuated hours ago, desks cleared, computers dark, fifty-six years of rock radio reduced to boxes in a hallway waiting for someone to decide what gets saved and what gets thrown away.

My hands rest on the console. Steady. That's the thing about guilt—you carry it long enough, it stops shaking you. It just sits there, heavy and permanent, like scar tissue around your heart.

I cue "Bohemian Rhapsody." The full six minutes, no radio edit. Because tonight we have time. Tomorrow we have nothing.

---

The Battle of the Bands was my idea.

Not mine alone—Tom Andrews and I pitched it together in the fall of 1978. Regional high school competition, WBCN sponsorship, prize money and a recording session for the winners. We sold it to management as a marketing campaign: discover the next Aerosmith before they need us, drive listeners in the 15-25 demographic, attract sponsors who wanted access to that audience.

It made sense. Corporate consolidation was already starting—you could feel it coming like weather, the way playlists were tightening, the way management kept talking about demographics instead of just playing music that mattered. The station needed money to stay independent. I thought I could game the system. Use capitalism to fund rebellion.

I'd discovered Aerosmith in 1973. Broke The Cars when they were still playing dive bars in Cambridge. Gave Boston their first airtime when everyone else thought they were too polished. I had the track record. I had the ear. I thought I could make stars, control outcomes, find lightning and bottle it.

The Battle of the Bands was supposed to prove that. Marketing genius wrapped in artistic legitimacy. Find talent, give them a platform, turn a high school talent show into something that mattered.

I thought I was the architect of success.

Turns out I was the architect of tragedy.

---

March 15, 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium, 985 seats packed with people who'd chosen sides before the first note was played. I sat in the judge's panel between two other WBCN DJs, clipboard in hand, trying to look professional while watching something die in real time.

Nick Johnson's band—Walking the Line—four kids from the northeast neighborhoods with duct-taped equipment and more hunger than technical skill. They played "Walk This Way" like their lives depended on it, because maybe they did. I could see Grace Johnson in the third row, still wearing her Friendly's uniform, hands gripped together in her lap like she was praying.

Jackie Marsh's band—Crown Jewels—four kids with professional equipment and the kind of technical precision that comes from expensive lessons and parents who can afford to care about things beyond making rent. They played "Bohemian Rhapsody" flawlessly. Every note perfect. Every harmony arranged. Empty as a mansion with no one home.

The crowd wasn't divided the way I'd expected. That was the strange part. Kids from all four quadrants—Rampers, Rats, Regs, Rollers—mixed together for the first time, choosing Aerosmith or Queen instead of zip codes. But they were still choosing sides. Still making it a war. Just different battle lines than the ones Sudbury had drawn for them.

Nick and Jackie didn't look at each other. Not once. Not during setup, not during performances, not when it was over and the damage was done.

I watched their friendship continue to drown in front of 985 witnesses. Public execution disguised as competition. And I'd sold the tickets.

---

Here's what I tell myself: I didn't create their division.

High school did that. Hop Brook geography did that. Dan Johnson's death in November 1977 did that—grief builds walls faster than friendship can climb them. Dr. Marsh's pressure on Jackie did that. Class warfare did that. America did that.

Two boys who once harmonized so perfectly it made their eighth-grade music teacher stop mid-sentence, stand there with her baton frozen, and realize she'd been teaching notes when these kids were making something that couldn't be taught—they'd been drifting apart for years. The labyrinth was killing them slowly. Private tragedy, the kind that happens to friendships every day. They might have found their way back to each other eventually, or they might not have. That's how innocence dies—quietly, gradually, in the spaces between conversations that never happen.

But I took that slow, private death and turned it into public spectacle. I saw two boys drifting apart and said, "Let's make them fight on stage. For sponsors. For content. For money."

I didn't kill their friendship. But I gave class warfare a microphone. I sold tickets to watch innocence die. I turned tragedy into entertainment.

And then I called it opportunity.

The Battle of the Bands was supposed to prove that. Marketing genius wrapped in artistic legitimacy. Find talent, give them a platform, turn a high school talent show into something that mattered.

I thought I was the architect of success.

Turns out I was the architect of tragedy.

---

March 15, 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium, 985 seats packed with people who'd chosen sides before the first note was played. I sat in the judge's panel between two other WBCN DJs, clipboard in hand, trying to look professional while watching something die in real time.

Nick Johnson's band—Walking the Line—four kids from the northeast neighborhoods with duct-taped equipment and more hunger than technical skill. They played "Walk This Way" like their lives depended on it, because maybe they did. I could see Grace Johnson in the third row, still wearing her Friendly's uniform, hands gripped together in her lap like she was praying.

Jackie Marsh's band—Crown Jewels—four kids with professional equipment and the kind of technical precision that comes from expensive lessons and parents who can afford to care about things beyond making rent. They played "Bohemian Rhapsody" flawlessly. Every note perfect. Every harmony arranged. Empty as a mansion with no one home.

The crowd wasn't divided the way I'd expected. That was the strange part. Kids from all four quadrants—Rampers, Rats, Regs, Rollers—mixed together for the first time, choosing Aerosmith or Queen instead of zip codes. But they were still choosing sides. Still making it a war. Just different battle lines than the ones Sudbury had drawn for them.

Nick and Jackie didn't look at each other. Not once. Not during setup, not during performances, not when it was over and the damage was done.

I watched their friendship continue to drown in front of 985 witnesses. Public execution disguised as competition. And I'd sold the tickets.

---

Here's what I tell myself: I didn't create their division.

High school did that. Hop Brook geography did that. Dan Johnson's death in November 1977 did that—grief builds walls faster than friendship can climb them. Dr. Marsh's pressure on Jackie did that. Class warfare did that. America did that.

Two boys who once harmonized so perfectly it made their eighth-grade music teacher stop mid-sentence, stand there with her baton frozen, and realize she'd been teaching notes when these kids were making something that couldn't be taught—they'd been drifting apart for years. The labyrinth was killing them slowly. Private tragedy, the kind that happens to friendships every day. They might have found their way back to each other eventually, or they might not have. That's how innocence dies—quietly, gradually, in the spaces between conversations that never happen.

But I took that slow, private death and turned it into public spectacle. I saw two boys drifting apart and said, "Let's make them fight on stage. For sponsors. For content. For money."

I didn't kill their friendship. But I gave class warfare a microphone. I sold tickets to watch innocence die. I turned tragedy into entertainment.

And then I called it opportunity.

---

I left WBCN in 1980. One year after the Battle. Exactly one year.

The official reason was career advancement. Danny Goldberg's management company offered me a job doing national tour promotion. More money, more influence, more power to shape careers from the industry side instead of the radio side. Record label A&R work, artist management, the kind of position that meant I'd made it.

I told everyone it was the logical next step. Ten years breaking bands on-air, now I'd help them from behind the scenes. Still in music, just a different angle. People congratulated me. Tom Andrews threw me a going-away party.

But here's what I knew, sitting in this booth on my last night in 1980, watching the sun come up over Boston:

I was fleeing.

Not from failure—from success. The Battle of the Bands had been successful. Great turnout, ratings up, coverage in the Globe. Strong sponsorship, management wanted to make it annual. I'd proven I could turn content into money, tragedy into product.

And I couldn't face what I'd become.

Corporate consolidation was accelerating. I could see the future: playlists, safe choices, rebellion as branding. WBCN would survive by compromising, gradually, until the rebel station became just another frequency selling nostalgia for what it used to be.

I left before I had to compromise. I thought that was the smart choice. I thought leaving meant I'd preserved something pure.

Forty-four years later, I can see the truth: Leaving was the compromise. I traded my voice for survival. I went corporate. I became what I fought. Just quietly. Just gradually. Just the same as if I'd stayed.

---

The song reaches the opera section. Freddie Mercury's voice soars through Studio B, filling the empty station with sound that cost someone everything to create ((purple prose at the end here, EDIT!)). He died in 1991. AIDS, thirty years of medicine too late. Another casualty of a world that punishes people for being what they are.

I take another sip of bourbon. Tyler's gift, nearly half a century old, tastes like regret.((NO NO NO NO no more Steven Tyler, or Bourbon this is so overplayed!))

Forty-four years in corporate music. A&R, promotion, artist management. I helped bands get signed—the safe ones, the ones that fit the formula, the ones that wouldn't challenge anything. I survived by becoming the machinery. ((GREAT!!))

I told myself I was still in music. Still helping artists. Still connected to what mattered. ((great!!))

But I wasn't on-air. I wasn't speaking. I'd gone silent. ((great!!))

The rebel DJ who turned the volume to full and didn't give a damn what anyone thought became a corporate suit who measured risk and calculated demographics and helped turn art into product.((great!!))

I survived. Nick and Jackie didn't—their potential erased, their friendship killed, their music silenced. WBCN survived until 2024, compromising gradually until corporate consolidation killed it anyway. ((great))


Three casualties of the same war. Three different strategies. Same outcome.

Nick stayed real. The system crushed him.

Jackie compromised. The system crushed him.

I fled. The system followed me.

The labyrinth has no exit. Fight, compromise, or run—you die regardless. Just different timelines. Just different flavors of the same defeat. ((great!!))

---

"Bohemian Rhapsody" builds toward the rock section. "So you think you can stone me and spit in my eye..."

I know why the station brought me back. Not for nostalgia week. Not to "celebrate" forty-four years of rock radio before corporate overlords flip the switch.

They brought me back because I'm the mirror. The cautionary tale. The one who left in 1980 and went corporate and survived by becoming complicit.

Look what you became, the empty station says. You left. We stayed. We all died anyway. Now tell that story on your way out. Confession disguised as celebration. ((great!! gave me chills!))

I could have said no. I'd been silent for forty-four years. Why come back?

Because the station's death gives me permission. You can't fire someone from a corpse. You can't blacklist someone when the industry's already dead. This is my last chance to break forty-four years of silence. To tell the truth about what I did. What we all did.

Not redemption. I can't undo March 15, 1979 ((we should date check the novel as I think some say March, some say May )). I can't bring back Nick and Jackie's friendship. I can't restore WBCN's rebel soul. I can't un-become what I became.

Just confession. Just witness. Just: This is what I did. This is what my ambition cost. This is what we lose when we turn children into content, friendship into competition, art into product.

The labyrinth wins. Always. That's not a question. ((great!))

But someone has to say it out loud. Someone has to document what we kill. Someone has to refuse to let the machinery erase even the memory of what existed before we destroyed it.((great))

That's all I have. It's not redemption. It's not hope. It's not even resistance. ((great))

It's just: I saw it. I participated. And before the lights go out, I'm telling you what we did.

---

The song ends. Six minutes of Freddie Mercury's genius, fading to silence in an empty station.

I lean into the microphone. The ON AIR light pulses like a heartbeat ((we have used this "pulses like a heartbeat before, need something creative and new))running out of time.

"May 9th, 1979," I say. "Twenty-four hours before the Battle of the Bands. My Battle. My idea. My destruction." ((not our dates ae may! anyway, we can come back later and fix the dates we can work on the prose and the chpaters now if Scalpel gets back on the job.))

My voice is steady. Forty-four years of practice at not shaking.

"Two boys in different rooms. Nick Johnson in his garage on Dutton Road, surrounded by his dead father's tools. Jackie Marsh in his basement studio, surrounded by his father's expectations. Both carrying more weight than any seventeen-year-old should carry. Both making choices they didn't understand yet. Both heading toward a stage I built for them."

I reach for the next cart. "Dream On." Aerosmith. The band that made me believe I was magic.

"Neither of them knowing what I'd created. What I'd done to their friendship. What the labyrinth does to innocence. Every time. Forever."

I press play.

"This is 'Dream On.' The band I discovered in 1973. The band that proved I had the ear. The band that made me think I could control outcomes."

Steven Tyler's voice fills the booth. That opening piano, haunting and pure, from back when they were nobody and I gave them everything. ((pretty darn egotistic, is that who she is now?))

"Twenty-four hours before I learned I couldn't save anyone."

I sit back. The bourbon glass catches the red glow of the ON AIR light. ((SCALPEL, what happened, why the bourbon again again again ???))

"Including myself."

Outside the booth, the station is empty—everyone evacuated hours ago, desks cleared, computers dark, fifty-six years of rock radio reduced to boxes in a hallway waiting for someone to decide what gets saved and what gets thrown away.

My hands rest on the console. Steady. That's the thing about guilt—you carry it long enough, it stops shaking you. It just sits there, heavy and permanent, like scar tissue around your heart.

I cue "Bohemian Rhapsody." The full six minutes, no radio edit. Because tonight we have time. Tomorrow we have nothing.

---

The Battle of the Bands was my idea.

Not mine alone—Tom Andrews and I pitched it together in the fall of 1978. Regional high school competition, WBCN sponsorship, prize money and a recording session for the winners. We sold it to management as a marketing campaign: discover the next Aerosmith before they need us, drive listeners in the 15-25 demographic, attract sponsors who wanted access to that audience.

It made sense. Corporate consolidation was already starting—you could feel it coming like weather, the way playlists were tightening, the way management kept talking about demographics instead of just playing music that mattered. The station needed money to stay independent. I thought I could game the system. Use capitalism to fund rebellion.

I'd discovered Aerosmith in 1973. Broke The Cars when they were still playing dive bars in Cambridge. Gave Boston their first airtime when everyone else thought they were too polished. I had the track record. I had the ear. I thought I could make stars, control outcomes, find lightning and bottle it.

The Battle of the Bands was supposed to prove that. Marketing genius wrapped in artistic legitimacy. Find talent, give them a platform, turn a high school talent show into something that mattered.

I thought I was the architect of success.

Turns out I was the architect of tragedy.

---

March 15, 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium, 985 seats packed with people who'd chosen sides before the first note was played. I sat in the judge's panel between two other WBCN DJs, clipboard in hand, trying to look professional while watching something die in real time.

Nick Johnson's band—Walking the Line—four kids from the northeast neighborhoods with duct-taped equipment and more hunger than technical skill. They played "Walk This Way" like their lives depended on it, because maybe they did. I could see Grace Johnson in the third row, still wearing her Friendly's uniform, hands gripped together in her lap like she was praying.

Jackie Marsh's band—Crown Jewels—four kids with professional equipment and the kind of technical precision that comes from expensive lessons and parents who can afford to care about things beyond making rent. They played "Bohemian Rhapsody" flawlessly. Every note perfect. Every harmony arranged. Empty as a mansion with no one home.

The crowd wasn't divided the way I'd expected. That was the strange part. Kids from all four quadrants—Rampers, Rats, Regs, Rollers—mixed together for the first time, choosing Aerosmith or Queen instead of zip codes. But they were still choosing sides. Still making it a war. Just different battle lines than the ones Sudbury had drawn for them.

Nick and Jackie didn't look at each other. Not once. Not during setup, not during performances, not when it was over and the damage was done.

I watched their friendship continue to drown in front of 985 witnesses. Public execution disguised as competition. And I'd sold the tickets.

---

Here's what I tell myself: I didn't create their division.

High school did that. Hop Brook geography did that. Dan Johnson's death in November 1977 did that—grief builds walls faster than friendship can climb them. Dr. Marsh's pressure on Jackie did that. Class warfare did that. America did that.

Two boys who once harmonized so perfectly it made their eighth-grade music teacher stop mid-sentence, stand there with her baton frozen, and realize she'd been teaching notes when these kids were making something that couldn't be taught—they'd been drifting apart for years. The labyrinth was killing them slowly. Private tragedy, the kind that happens to friendships every day. They might have found their way back to each other eventually, or they might not have. That's how innocence dies—quietly, gradually, in the spaces between conversations that never happen.

But I took that slow, private death and turned it into public spectacle. I saw two boys drifting apart and said, "Let's make them fight on stage. For sponsors. For content. For money."

I didn't kill their friendship. But I gave class warfare a microphone. I sold tickets to watch innocence die. I turned tragedy into entertainment.

And then I called it opportunity.

---

I left WBCN in 1980. One year after the Battle. Exactly one year.

The official reason was career advancement. Danny Goldberg's management company offered me a job doing national tour promotion. More money, more influence, more power to shape careers from the industry side instead of the radio side. Record label A&R work, artist management, the kind of position that meant I'd made it.

I told everyone it was the logical next step. Ten years breaking bands on-air, now I'd help them from behind the scenes. Still in music, just a different angle. People congratulated me. Tom Andrews threw me a going-away party.

But here's what I knew, sitting in this booth on my last night in 1980, watching the sun come up over Boston:

I was fleeing.

Not from failure—from success. The Battle of the Bands had been successful. Great turnout, ratings up, coverage in the Globe. Strong sponsorship, management wanted to make it annual. I'd proven I could turn content into money, tragedy into product.

And I couldn't face what I'd become.

Corporate consolidation was accelerating. I could see the future: playlists, safe choices, rebellion as branding. WBCN would survive by compromising, gradually, until the rebel station became just another frequency selling nostalgia for what it used to be.

I left before I had to compromise. I thought that was the smart choice. I thought leaving meant I'd preserved something pure.

Forty-four years later, I can see the truth: Leaving was the compromise. I traded my voice for survival. I went corporate. I became what I fought. Just quietly. Just gradually. Just the same as if I'd stayed.

---

The song reaches the opera section. Freddie Mercury's voice fills Studio B. He died in 1991. AIDS, thirty years of medicine too late. Another casualty of a world that punishes people for being what they are.

The clock on the wall says 11:47 PM. Thirteen minutes left.

Forty-four years in corporate music. A&R, promotion, artist management. I helped bands get signed—the safe ones, the ones that fit the formula, the ones that wouldn't challenge anything. I survived by becoming the machinery. ((GREAT!!))

I told myself I was still in music. Still helping artists. Still connected to what mattered. ((great!!))

But I wasn't on-air. I wasn't speaking. I'd gone silent. ((great!!))

The rebel DJ who turned the volume to full and didn't give a damn what anyone thought became a corporate suit who measured risk and calculated demographics and helped turn art into product.((great!!))

I survived. Nick and Jackie didn't—their potential erased, their friendship killed, their music silenced. WBCN survived until 2024, compromising gradually until corporate consolidation killed it anyway. ((great))


Three casualties of the same war. Three different strategies. Same outcome.

Nick stayed real. The system crushed him.

Jackie compromised. The system crushed him.

I fled. The system followed me.

The labyrinth has no exit. Fight, compromise, or run—you die regardless. Just different timelines. Just different flavors of the same defeat. ((great!!))

---

"Bohemian Rhapsody" builds toward the rock section. "So you think you can stone me and spit in my eye..."

I know why the station brought me back. Not for nostalgia week. Not to "celebrate" fifty-six years of rock radio before corporate overlords flip the switch.

They brought me back because I'm the mirror. The cautionary tale. The one who left in 1980 and went corporate and survived by becoming complicit.

Look what you became, the empty station says. You left. We stayed. We all died anyway. Now tell that story on your way out. Confession disguised as celebration.

I could have said no. I'd been silent for forty-four years. Why come back?

Because the station's death gives me permission. You can't fire someone from a corpse. You can't blacklist someone when the industry's already dead. This is my last chance to break forty-four years of silence. To tell the truth about what I did. What we all did.

Not redemption. I can't undo May 9th, 1979. I can't bring back Nick and Jackie's friendship. I can't restore WBCN's rebel soul. I can't un-become what I became.

Just confession. Just witness. Just: This is what I did. This is what my ambition cost. This is what we lose when we turn children into content, friendship into competition, art into product.

The labyrinth wins. Always. That's not a question. ((great!))

But someone has to say it out loud. Someone has to document what we kill. Someone has to refuse to let the machinery erase even the memory of what existed before we destroyed it.((great))

That's all I have. It's not redemption. It's not hope. It's not even resistance. ((great))

It's just: I saw it. I participated. And before the lights go out, I'm telling you what we did.

---

The song ends. Six minutes of Freddie Mercury's genius, fading to silence in an empty station.

I lean into the microphone. The ON AIR light burns steady above the door.

"May 9th, 1979," I say. "Twenty-four hours before the Battle of the Bands. My Battle. My idea. My destruction."

My voice is steady. Forty-four years of practice at not shaking.

"Two boys in different rooms. Nick Johnson in his garage on Dutton Road, surrounded by his dead father's tools. Jackie Marsh in his basement studio, surrounded by his father's expectations. Both carrying more weight than any seventeen-year-old should carry. Both making choices they didn't understand yet. Both heading toward a stage I built for them."

I reach for the next cart. "Dream On." Aerosmith. The band I discovered in 1973.

"Neither of them knowing what I'd created. What I'd done to their friendship. What the labyrinth does to innocence. Every time. Forever."

I press play.

"This is 'Dream On.' The band that proved I had the ear. The band that made me think I could control outcomes."

The opening piano fills the booth. Haunting and pure.

"Twenty-four hours before I learned I couldn't save anyone."

I watch the clock tick toward midnight.

"Including myself."

## THE BREAKTHROUGH: "SCALPEL & HOSE" METHODOLOGY

### **Origin (Chapter 21):**
User explicitly requested: "SCALPEL has been superb cutting garbage, repetitive wording and purple prose. This is EXACTLY what this novel needs. BUT Author challenges Scalpel to also look for ways to bolster the prose and story with additional helpful and relevant scenes knowing the whole scope of the story."

**The Naming:** User coined "Scalpel and Hose" as "Blood Brothers"
- **Scalpel:** Cuts garbage, repetition, purple prose (what I'd been doing)
- **Hose:** Adds scenes that deepen character, raise stakes, earn emotion (new addition)

### **The Character Depth Hierarchy (Universal Framework):**

**TIER 1 - MAIN CHARACTERS:**
Nick, Jackie, Grace, Maxanne, Dr. Marsh
- ALWAYS explore motivation for key decisions
- We see the COST of their choices
- Internal conflict shown through action + brief internal moment
- One internal "why" moment per chapter

**TIER 2 - SUPPORTING CHARACTERS:**
Stephen, Mark, David, Patty, Elizabeth, Tom Andrews, Bob Wentworth
- ONE defining moment each
- Shows WHY they matter to the story
- Reveals character through specific detail, not explanation

**TIER 3 - BACKGROUND:**
Dr. Taub, other teachers, town gossips, PTA parents
- Action only, no motivation
- They're FORCES, not people
- Concrete details (what they wear, how they talk) but no internal life

**THE RULE:**
"If a character makes a choice that affects the plot, we see WHY. If they're backdrop, we see WHAT."

## THEMATIC FRAMEWORK: GREEK TRAGEDY + LOSS OF INNOCENCE

### **Core Discussion (Chapter 23 Development):**
User questioned whether Greek Tragedy framework conflicted with "Loss of Innocence" theme.

**Resolution:** They're the same thing in modern context.

**Traditional Greek Tragedy:**
- Gods (fate) control outcome
- Heroes can't escape destiny
- Tragic flaw leads to downfall
- Recognition comes too late
- Audience experiences catharsis

**"Walk This Way" Modern Parallel:**
- Gods = Corporate system / Class warfare (faceless, all-powerful)
- Heroes = Nick, Jackie, Maxanne, WBCN (can't escape the machine)
- Tragic flaw = Believing music could save them (hubris)
- Recognition = Maxanne seeing the parallel (anagnorisis)
- Catharsis = Telling the truth (not redemption—witness)

**Loss of Innocence = Inevitable:**
- Labyrinth kills innocence (always)
- System destroys purity on contact
- Nick/Jackie couldn't escape (too young, too pure)
- WBCN couldn't escape (corporate consolidation)
- Maxanne couldn't escape (fled but system followed)

**The Message (Pure Tragedy):**
"The labyrinth wins. Always. That's not a question. But someone has to say it out loud. Someone has to document what we kill. Someone has to refuse to let the machinery erase even the memory of what existed before we destroyed it. That's all I have. It's not redemption. It's not hope. It's not even resistance. It's just: I saw it. I participated. And before the lights go out, I'm telling you what we did."

**User's Decision:** "I am 100% okay with the tragedy ending... if adding hope softens the blow then let's not add that in."

**No False Hope. Pure Tragedy. Just Witness.**

## WHAT WORKS WELL: THE SCALPEL & HOSE PHILOSOPHY

### **Why This Methodology Succeeded:**

**1. DUAL ACTION - Simultaneous Cut & Build:**
- Traditional editing = cut bad prose OR add depth (one at a time)
- Scalpel & Hose = do BOTH in same pass
- Result: Chapters get tighter AND deeper simultaneously
- Efficiency: One pass achieves two goals

**2. CHARACTER DEPTH HIERARCHY - Universal Framework:**
- Clear tiers eliminate guesswork (TIER 1 = always show motivation, TIER 2 = one defining moment, TIER 3 = forces only)
- Applicable to ANY novel (not specific to this story)
- Prevents flat characters, clichés, cardboard cutouts
- Answer to critics: "characters need more depth"

**3. SPECIFIC QUESTIONS DRIVE DEPTH:**
For TIER 1 characters, ask:
- What is their SPECIFIC fear? (not "worried" but exact fear)
- What is the COST of their choice? (what they sacrifice/lose)
- What is their MOTIVATION? (why this choice, not another)
- What is their internal "WHY" moment? (brief glimpse inside)

**4. EARNED EMOTION THROUGH SPECIFICITY:**
- Don't name emotion ("Jackie was nervous")
- Show through specific detail ("Jackie's fingers tight on guitar strap")
- Don't explain theme ("class warfare divides")
- Show through concrete moment (cafeteria geography, Friendly's uniform, equipment cost)

**5. BRUTAL HONESTY ACCEPTED:**
- Agent must ACKNOWLEDGE failures, not defend them
- "Scalpel, what happened?" → "You're right. I got lazy. Here's the fix."
- Shame list = accountability
- User trusts agent who admits mistakes

**6. USER'S VOICE PRESERVED:**
- `(())` system keeps user's emotional response in text
- "yuck!!!" and "great!!" guide revision priorities
- Agent learns user's aesthetic through accumulation
- Shared vocabulary builds over sessions

**7. SYSTEMATIC APPLICATION:**
- Not random "make it better"
- Methodical: Read → Assess → Cut 50% → Add depth where needed
- Checklist approach (TIER 1 checklist, purple prose checklist, timeline checklist)
- Repeatable across chapters

**8. TRUST + VERIFICATION:**
- User trusts agent to make prose decisions within constraints
- Agent provides detailed explanations for changes
- User verifies with `(())` comments
- Collaborative, not dictatorial

**9. MEMORY ACROSS CHAPTERS:**
- Track repetitive words (callused, sawdust, bourbon)
- Maintain timeline consistency
- Reference earlier chapters for voice calibration
- Build patterns recognition over sessions

**10. FOCUS ON READER EXPERIENCE:**
- "Trust the reader" = core principle
- Don't over-explain themes
- Show, don't tell
- If you're tempted to explain, you're overwriting

## LESSONS LEARNED (October 21, 2025 Session)

### **What Worked:**
1. **Scalpel & Hose dual methodology** - revolutionary for efficiency and quality
2. **Character Depth Hierarchy** - solved "flat character" problem systematically
3. **Brutal honesty** - user calling out failures led to best revisions
4. **`(())` feedback system** - highly efficient, contextual, emotional
5. **Money sentences concept** - 4-6 sentences per chapter that "earn their place"
6. **Greek Tragedy framework** - aligned perfectly with Loss of Innocence theme
7. **"Continue to drown" instead of "die"** - user's specific word choice improved metaphor
8. **Replacing clichés with earned moments** - "made teachers cry" → specific frozen-baton moment

### **What Failed (Then Got Fixed):**
1. **Purple prose creep** - got drunk on own writing in Ch 23 draft 1
2. **Bourbon/Tyler repetition** - didn't track across chapters, used 4x in one chapter
3. **Plot accuracy** - revealed Nick wins (spoiler), contradicted crowd dynamics
4. **Timeline laziness** - guessed at years (44 vs 56), didn't verify math
5. **Lazy clichés** - "made teachers cry" = shortcut, not earned
6. **Egotistic prose** - "I gave them everything" = Maxanne wouldn't think this way

**Key Learning:** When user says "Time for Scalpel to rise from the ashes!" → they're right. Accept it. Fix it. Don't defend garbage.

### **For Future Sessions:**
- Continue `(())` system
- Apply Scalpel & Hose to ALL remaining chapters
- Track repetitive words systematically (create running list)
- Always verify timeline/plot details (don't guess)
- Remember: User prefers "improved/tightened" over "polished"
- Ask "What is the COST?" for every TIER 1 character choice
- Cut first, then add depth (Scalpel, then Hose)
- Money sentences: 4-6 per chapter that hit hard

- Reveals character through specific detail

- Concrete details but no internal life

```plaintext
CHAPTER 24: THE WITNESS

---

May 9th, 1979. St. Michael's Church, Concord.

Patty Lally sat alone in the empty sanctuary, a cassette tape in her hands. Camp Winaukee, Summer 1975, written in her fourteen-year-old handwriting on the label. Four years old. Might as well be four decades.

She'd been carrying this tape in her backpack for three weeks, ever since she'd heard about the Battle of the Bands. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional, Friday night, WBCN sponsorship, the whole town choosing sides. Working-class Aerosmith versus upper-class Queen. Nick Johnson versus Jackie Marsh.

The boys who used to be brothers.

She pressed play. The tape hissed, then: three voices harmonizing on "Your Song," Elton John filtered through something that couldn't be taught. Nick's guitar, raw and honest. Jackie's piano, precise and pure. Her voice, finding the melody that connected them.

They'd recorded this on the last night of camp, Mr. Freedman's boom box balanced on a picnic table by the lake. They'd made promises that night. Stay in touch. Form a band. Change the world.

She'd kept her half. Wrote Nick in September. Wrote Jackie in October. Wrote them both every month through freshman year.

Neither one ever wrote back.

Patty stopped the tape. Four years of silence, and now they were going to war. On stage. In front of the whole town. Making the division permanent.

She wasn't going to save them. You can't save people who've already chosen.

But she could make them see the cost.

---

Dutton Road, Sudbury. Northeast quadrant. The address was still in her camp notebook.

The garage door was open. Nick Johnson stood alone with his guitar, playing "Dream On" to an audience of Dan Johnson's tools. The solo his father taught him, note-perfect, heartbreaking.

Patty watched from the driveway. He'd gotten taller, shoulders broader from construction work he'd taken on after his father died. But his hands on the guitar—those were the same hands from camp. Before they'd learned to grip so tight.

"You're playing like you're trying to prove something," she said.

Nick's fingers stopped. He turned. Stared.

"Patty?"

"At camp, you played like you had nothing to prove." She walked into the garage, stopped ten feet away. "That's the difference between real and desperate."

Nick's face went through several expressions—surprise, confusion, something that might have been shame. "What are you doing here?"

"I came to see what you've become."

"I'm fine. Busy. Senior year, you know—"

"I wrote you letters." Flat. No emotion. Just fact. "Seventeen letters over two years. You never wrote back."

Nick set the guitar down. "Patty, it's not—look, things got complicated. Jackie's dad, the class stuff at school, Dan dying—"

"I know about your father. I'm sorry." She meant it. "But that's not why you stopped writing. You stopped because writing to me meant admitting you were still the person from camp. And you couldn't be that person anymore. Not in Sudbury."

"You don't understand what it's like here—"

"No. I understand exactly." She pulled out the cassette tape. "I understand that you and Jackie were brothers. I understand that you made something real. And I understand that you let them turn you into symbols. Working-class hero versus privileged perfectionist. Aerosmith versus Queen. The garage versus the mansion."

She held up the tape. "This is what you were. Want to hear it?"

Nick looked at the tape like it was evidence at a crime scene. "I don't—"

"Tomorrow night, I'm entering the Battle." She put the tape back in her pocket. "Not to fix you. Not to make you friends again. To show everyone what you threw away. What brotherhood looked like before Sudbury divided it into territories."

"Patty—"

"I'm not asking for anything, Nick. I'm telling you. Tomorrow night, when you're on that stage proving you're more authentic than Jackie, more real than his classical training, more working-class than his privilege—I want you to remember this tape. Remember that you used to play music because it made you feel something. Not because it proved something."

She turned to leave. Stopped at the garage door.

"Your father was right. Music doesn't care where you come from. But you forgot the second half of that lesson. Music also doesn't care what you're trying to prove. It just cares if you're telling the truth."

She walked away. Didn't look back. Behind her, the garage stayed silent.

---

The Marsh house looked like something from a catalog. Colonial architecture, circular driveway, lawn maintained by people who got paid to care about grass.

Patty rang the doorbell.

A girl answered. Thirteen, maybe fourteen. Dark hair, violin case leaning against the wall behind her.

"I'm looking for Jackie," Patty said.

The girl studied her. "You're Patty Lally."

"How do you—"

"Jackie talked about you. After camp. For months." The girl stepped aside. "I'm Elizabeth. His sister. He's in the basement."

Patty followed her inside. The house smelled like furniture polish and expectations.

"He doesn't talk about you anymore," Elizabeth said, leading her down carpeted stairs. "He doesn't talk about Nick either. It's like that summer never happened."

"I know."

"But it did happen, right? They really were friends?"

"Yes."

Elizabeth stopped at the basement door. "Good. I wanted to make sure I wasn't imagining it. That he used to be different."

She opened the door. Left Patty alone at the top of the stairs.

The basement had been converted into a practice studio. Soundproofing, professional equipment, a Steinway baby grand that cost more than Grace Johnson's car. Jackie sat at the piano, playing "Bohemian Rhapsody" with technical perfection and zero breath.

Patty descended. Her footsteps silent on the carpeted stairs.

Jackie's hands stopped when he saw her reflection in the piano's polished surface.

"Hello, Jackie."

He turned slowly. Pale. "Patty? What—how did you get in?"

"Elizabeth let me in. She's worried about you."

"I'm fine—"

"You're not playing music. You're executing it." She crossed to the piano, pulled out the cassette tape. "Remember this?"

Jackie stared at the tape. Something crossed his face—recognition, loss, fear.

"Camp Winaukee," Patty said. "Final night. The three of us by the lake. You played piano like you were breathing. Not performing. Not proving. Just breathing."

"That was a long time ago—"

"Four years. I wrote you letters. You never wrote back."

Jackie stood. "Patty, I'm sorry. I was—things got busy. My father wanted me to focus on college prep, classical competitions—"

"Your father counts notes like credits on a transcript." She held his eyes. "You used to make music. Now you're just collecting approval. Which one of you am I talking to—you or him?"

Jackie's jaw tightened. "You don't know what it's like. The pressure, the expectations—"

"You're right. I don't know what it's like in your house." She gestured at the studio. "But I know what it's like to make music that matters. We did it together. Remember?"

She set the tape on the piano. "Tomorrow night, I'm entering the Battle. I'll play this for everyone. Original songs, the way we said we would. No covers. No proving who's more authentic or more technical. Just truth."

"Patty—"

"I'm not here to save you, Jackie. You and Nick made your choices. You let Sudbury's invisible lines become visible walls. You let your friendship become a war." She headed for the stairs. "Tomorrow night, I'll show everyone what you had before you chose this. Then you can live with what you picked instead."

She climbed the stairs. Stopped halfway.

"At camp, when we harmonized, you said it felt like flying. Remember that? You said classical music was your father's language, but rock was yours. You said playing Queen made you feel like you could breathe."

Jackie stood frozen at the piano.

"Tomorrow night," Patty said, "I'll be breathing. While you and Nick suffocate in the roles Sudbury gave you, I'll be reminding everyone what air tastes like."

She left. Elizabeth was waiting at the top of the stairs.

"Did you fix him?" the girl asked.

"No. You can't fix people who don't want to be fixed."

"Then why did you come?"

Patty looked back down the stairs. Jackie was sitting at the piano again, staring at the cassette tape.

"Because someone has to witness what they lost. Someone has to say: This is what brotherhood looked like. This is what they chose instead. So when they're old and wondering what happened, they'll remember someone was there. Someone saw. Someone documented the cost."

---

St. Michael's Church. Evening.

Patty sat alone in the sanctuary, the cassette tape on the pew beside her.

Tomorrow night, she'd walk onto that stage in Sudbury. Outsider in a war she hadn't started. Witness to a tragedy she couldn't stop.

She wasn't going to fix Nick and Jackie. The labyrinth had them now. Class warfare, parental pressure, grief, pride—all the machinery of division grinding friendship into dust.

But she could do what Maxanne Sartori had done with Aerosmith, with The Cars, with Boston. Play music that mattered. Music that didn't compete. Music that told the truth.

Nick and Jackie would be on that stage trying to prove they were better than each other. She'd be there proving music didn't care about better. It only cared about real.

They'd been real once. Three kids by a lake, making something beautiful because it was possible. Before Sudbury taught them it wasn't.

Tomorrow night, she'd remind everyone what possible looked like. What brotherhood sounded like before the world made it war.

Not to save them. They were already lost.

Just to document. To witness. To say: I saw what they were. This is what they became. Remember the difference.

The church was quiet except for the sound of her breathing.

Tomorrow, she'd make them listen. To what they'd thrown away. To what harmony cost when you chose division instead.

And then she'd leave them with their choice.

Because that's all a witness can do. Show the truth. Document the cost. Refuse to let them pretend it never happened.

The cassette tape sat on the pew. Evidence. Testimony. Proof.

Tomorrow night, the Battle of the Bands would crown a winner.

But Patty knew the truth: They'd already lost. All of them. The day friendship became competition.

She was just there to make sure someone remembered what losing looked like.

---

**END CHAPTER 24**

**Word Count: 1,780**

CHAPTER 24: THE RISER

---

May 9th, 1979. St. Michael's Church, Concord.

Patty Lally sat alone in the empty sanctuary, listening to the silence. Four years since Camp Winaukee. Four years since she'd written seven letters to two boys who never wrote back.

She'd been hearing about the Battle of the Bands for weeks. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional, Friday night, WBCN sponsorship, the whole town choosing sides. Working-class Aerosmith versus upper-class Queen. Nick Johnson versus Jackie Marsh.

The boys who used to be brothers.

Patty leaned back in the pew, stared at the stained glass above the altar. She could see what had happened to them. Nick trapped by grief, playing for his father's memory instead of with his father's joy. Jackie trapped by expectation, playing for approval instead of breath.

They were both trapped. Just in different cages.

She wasn't going to save them. You can't save people who've already chosen.

But she could show them what they were missing.

Tomorrow night, she'd walk onto that stage and play music the way it was meant to be played—not to prove anything, not to win anything, just because it made her alive.

She didn't care if she won. She just wanted to play.

---

Dutton Road, Sudbury. Northeast quadrant. The address was still in her camp notebook.

The garage door was open. Nick Johnson stood alone with his guitar, playing "Dream On" to an audience of Dan Johnson's tools. The solo his father taught him, note-perfect, heartbreaking.

Patty watched from the driveway. He'd gotten taller, shoulders broader from construction work he'd taken on after his father died. But his hands on the guitar—those were the same hands from camp. Before they'd learned to grip so tight.

"You're playing like you're trying to prove something," she said.

Nick's fingers stopped. He turned. Stared.

"Patty?"

"At camp, you played like you had nothing to prove." She walked into the garage, stopped ten feet away. "That's the difference between real and desperate."

Nick's face went through several expressions—surprise, confusion, something that might have been shame. "What are you doing here?"

"I came to see what you've become."

"I'm fine. Busy. Senior year, you know—"

"I wrote you letters." Flat. No emotion. Just fact. "Seventeen letters over two years. You never wrote back."

Nick set the guitar down. "Patty, it's not—look, things got complicated. Jackie's dad, the class stuff at school, Dan dying—"

"I know about your father. I'm sorry." She meant it. "But that's not why you stopped writing. You stopped because writing to me meant admitting you were still the person from camp. And you couldn't be that person anymore. Not in Sudbury."

"You don't understand what it's like here—"

"No. I understand exactly." She pulled out the cassette tape. "I understand that you and Jackie were brothers. I understand that you made something real. And I understand that you let them turn you into symbols. Working-class hero versus privileged perfectionist. Aerosmith versus Queen. The garage versus the mansion."

She held up the tape. "This is what you were. Want to hear it?"

Nick looked at the tape like it was evidence at a crime scene. "I don't—"

"Tomorrow night, I'm entering the Battle." She put the tape back in her pocket. "Not to fix you. Not to make you friends again. To show everyone what you threw away. What brotherhood looked like before Sudbury divided it into territories."

"Patty—"

"I'm not asking for anything, Nick. I'm telling you. Tomorrow night, when you're on that stage proving you're more authentic than Jackie, more real than his classical training, more working-class than his privilege—I want you to remember this tape. Remember that you used to play music because it made you feel something. Not because it proved something."

She turned to leave. Stopped at the garage door.

"Your father was right. Music doesn't care where you come from. But you forgot the second half of that lesson. Music also doesn't care what you're trying to prove. It just cares if you're telling the truth."

She walked away. Didn't look back. Behind her, the garage stayed silent.

---

The Marsh house looked like something from a catalog. Colonial architecture, circular driveway, lawn maintained by people who got paid to care about grass ((Scalpel we used thissimilar line earlier in the novel when we introduced the MArsh family, chapter 02)).

Patty rang the doorbell.

A girl answered. Thirteen, maybe fourteen. Dark hair, violin case leaning against the wall behind her.

"I'm looking for Jackie," Patty said.

The girl studied her. "You're Patty Lally."

"How do you—"

"Jackie talked about you. After camp. For months." The girl stepped aside. "I'm Elizabeth. His sister. He's in the basement."

Patty followed her inside. The house smelled like furniture polish and expectations.

"He doesn't talk about you anymore," Elizabeth said, leading her down carpeted stairs. "He doesn't talk about Nick either. It's like that summer never happened."

"I know."

"But it did happen, right? They really were friends?"

"Yes."

Elizabeth stopped at the basement door. "Good. I wanted to make sure I wasn't imagining it. That he used to be different."

She opened the door. Left Patty alone at the top of the stairs.

The basement had been converted into a practice studio. Soundproofing, professional equipment, a Steinway baby grand that cost more than Grace Johnson's car. Jackie sat at the piano, playing "Bohemian Rhapsody" with technical perfection and zero breath.

Patty descended. Her footsteps silent on the carpeted stairs.

Jackie's hands stopped when he saw her reflection in the piano's polished surface.

"Hello, Jackie."

He turned slowly. Pale. "Patty? What—how did you get in?"

"Elizabeth let me in. She's worried about you."

"I'm fine—"

"You're not playing music. You're executing it." She crossed to the piano, pulled out the cassette tape. "Remember this?"

Jackie stared at the tape. Something crossed his face—recognition, loss, fear.

"Camp Winaukee," Patty said. "Final night. The three of us by the lake. You played piano like you were breathing. Not performing. Not proving. Just breathing."

"That was a long time ago—"

"Four years. I wrote you letters. You never wrote back."

Jackie stood. "Patty, I'm sorry. I was—things got busy. My father wanted me to focus on college prep, classical competitions—"

"Your father counts notes like credits on a transcript." She held his eyes. "You used to make music. Now you're just collecting approval. Which one of you am I talking to—you or him ((we used simillar line earlier about the Dad counting like ... Dont need it"

Jackie's jaw tightened. "You don't know what it's like. The pressure, the expectations—"

"You're right. I don't know what it's like in your house." She gestured at the studio. "But I know what it's like to make music that matters. We did it together. Remember?"

She set the tape on the piano. "Tomorrow night, I'm entering the Battle. I'll play this for everyone. Original songs, the way we said we would. No covers. No proving who's more authentic or more technical. Just truth." ((I am not sure about the original songs, seems half-baked i was thinking they are all high school cover bands but you can argue the other way, undecided, I like PAtty and how you described her in the Greek Tragedy ... but bringing out an old tape and reminding the guys ... i might flip this on its head ... it's what she doesn't say that nick and jackie know is the truth, but she doesn't even have to be so deliberate, she can be, she can be just Patty on her terms))

"Patty—"

"I'm not here to save you, Jackie. You and Nick made your choices. You let Sudbury's invisible lines become visible walls. You let your friendship become a war." She headed for the stairs. "Tomorrow night, I'll show everyone what you had before you chose this. Then you can live with what you picked instead." ((seems preachy to me!  let's consider at least taking the opposite approach ... what would the restrained versio sound like .. what is PAtty's true intention, what is knawing at her? Unahppy family life and sje's trying to float above and not let others drag her down?  Not sure that fits with greek tragedy, just thinking out loud. Thoughts?))

She climbed the stairs. Stopped halfway.

"At camp, when we harmonized, you said it felt like flying. Remember that? You said classical music was your father's language, but rock was yours. You said playing Queen made you feel like you could breathe."

Jackie stood frozen at the piano.

"Tomorrow night," Patty said, "I'll be breathing. While you and Nick suffocate in the roles Sudbury ((I think it 's too much to bring "Sudbury" into the equation, to me it doesn't make sense here)) gave you, I'll be reminding everyone what air tastes like."

She left. Elizabeth was waiting at the top of the stairs.

"Did you fix him?" the girl asked.

"No. You can't fix people who don't want to be fixed."

"Then why did you come?"

Patty looked back down the stairs. Jackie was sitting at the piano again, staring at the cassette tape ((I would get rid of the damn tape, we got rid of one but another one back!)).

"Because someone has to witness what they lost. Someone has to say: This is what brotherhood looked like. This is what they chose instead. So when they're old and wondering what happened, they'll remember someone was there. Someone saw. Someone documented the cost."((yikes, a little over the top and "telling"))

---

St. Michael's Church. Evening.

Patty sat alone in the sanctuary, the cassette tape ((another tape, don't like it)) on the pew beside her.

Tomorrow night, she'd walk onto that stage in Sudbury. Outsider in a war she hadn't started. Witness to a tragedy she couldn't stop. ((good!))

She wasn't going to fix Nick and Jackie. The labyrinth had them now. Class warfare, parental pressure, grief, pride—all the machinery of division grinding friendship into dust.((good))

But she could do what Maxanne Sartori had done with Aerosmith, with The Cars, with Boston. Play music that mattered. Music that didn't compete. Music that told the truth. ((I would leave MAxanne out here, too convenient not believable from Patty))

Nick and Jackie would be on that stage trying to prove they were better than each other. She'd be there proving music didn't care about better. It only cared about real. ((okay))

They'd been real once. Three kids by a lake, making something beautiful because it was possible. Before Sudbury taught them it wasn't.((Dom't lean on sudbury!!  this doesn't feel real and to broad and just No))

Tomorrow night, she'd remind everyone what possible looked like. What brotherhood sounded like before the world made it war. ((okay))

Not to save them. They were already lost. ((okay))

Just to document. To witness. To say: I saw what they were. This is what they became. Remember the difference. ((okay, bit don't overdo it))

The church was quiet except for the sound of her breathing. ((nice))

Tomorrow, she'd make them listen. To what they'd thrown away. To what harmony cost when you chose division ((another word for division as we use this too much))instead.

And then she'd leave them with their choice. ((GREAT!))

Because that's all a witness can do. Show the truth. Document the cost. Refuse to let them pretend it never happened. ((maybe, can we frame this up in more relatable ways?  I get the point but this soujds like reading a biik on "Geek tragedy"))

The cassette tape sat on the pew. Evidence. Testimony. Proof. (( convenient))

Tomorrow night, the Battle of the Bands would crown a winner.

But Patty knew the truth: They'd already lost. All of them. The day friendship became competition.

She was just there to make sure someone remembered what losing looked like. ((really?? that's the reason she would be there?))

**END CHAPTER 24**

```plaintext
CHAPTER 24: THE RISER

---

May 9th, 1979. St. Michael's Church, Concord.

Patty Lally sat alone in the empty sanctuary, listening to the silence. Four years since Camp Winaukee. Four years since she'd written seven letters to two boys who never wrote back.

She'd been hearing about the Battle of the Bands for weeks. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional, Friday night, WBCN sponsorship, the whole town choosing sides. Working-class Aerosmith versus upper-class Queen. Nick Johnson versus Jackie Marsh.

The boys who used to be brothers.

Patty leaned back in the pew, stared at the stained glass above the altar. She could see what had happened to them. Nick trapped by grief, playing for his father's memory instead of with his father's joy. Jackie trapped by expectation, playing for approval instead of breath.

They were both trapped. Just in different cages.

She wasn't going to save them. You can't save people who've already chosen.

But she could show them what they were missing.

Tomorrow night, she'd walk onto that stage and play music the way it was meant to be played—not to prove anything, not to win anything, just because it made her alive.

She didn't care if she won. She just wanted to play.

---

Dutton Road, Sudbury. Northeast quadrant. The address was still in her camp notebook.

The garage door was open. Nick Johnson stood alone with his guitar, playing "Dream On" to an audience of Dan Johnson's tools. The solo his father taught him, note-perfect, heartbreaking.

Patty watched from the driveway. He'd gotten taller, shoulders broader from construction work he'd taken on after his father died. But his hands on the guitar—those were the same hands from camp. Before they'd learned to grip so tight.

"You're still playing 'Dream On,'" she said.

Nick's fingers stopped. He turned. Stared.

"Patty?"

"I wrote you seven times. You never wrote back."

Nick set the guitar down. "Patty, it's not—look, things got complicated. Jackie's dad, the class stuff at school, Dan dying—"

"You don't need to explain. I can see what happened here." She looked around the garage, at Dan's tools, at Nick's guitar. "You're playing for him now. Not with him."

Nick's face went through several expressions—surprise, confusion, something that might have been shame. "What are you doing here?"

"I came to see what you've become."

"I'm fine. Busy. Senior year, you know—"

"Tomorrow night, I'm entering the Battle." She turned to leave. "Not to fix you. Not to make you friends again. To show you what you're missing."

"Patty—"

She stopped at the garage door. "Your father was right. Music doesn't care where you come from. But you forgot the second half of that lesson. Music also doesn't care what you're trying to prove. It just cares if you're telling the truth."

She walked away. Didn't look back. Behind her, the garage stayed silent.

---

The Marsh house looked like something from a catalog. Colonial architecture, circular driveway, lawn maintained by people who got paid to care about grass.

Patty rang the doorbell.

A girl answered. Thirteen, maybe fourteen. Dark hair, violin case leaning against the wall behind her.

"I'm looking for Jackie," Patty said.

The girl studied her. "You're Patty Lally."

"How do you—"

"Jackie talked about you. After camp. For months." The girl stepped aside. "I'm Elizabeth. His sister. He's in the basement."

Patty followed her inside. The house smelled like furniture polish and expectations.

"He doesn't talk about you anymore," Elizabeth said, leading her down carpeted stairs. "He doesn't talk about Nick either. It's like that summer never happened."

"I know."

"But it did happen, right? They really were friends?"

"Yes."

Elizabeth stopped at the basement door. "Good. I wanted to make sure I wasn't imagining it. That he used to be different."

She opened the door. Left Patty alone at the top of the stairs.

The basement had been converted into a practice studio. Soundproofing, professional equipment, a Steinway baby grand that cost more than Grace Johnson's car. Jackie sat at the piano, playing "Bohemian Rhapsody" with technical perfection and zero breath.

Patty descended. Her footsteps silent on the carpeted stairs.

Jackie's hands stopped when he saw her reflection in the piano's polished surface.

"Hello, Jackie."

He turned slowly. Pale. "Patty? What—how did you get in?"

"Elizabeth let me in. She's worried about you."

"I'm fine—"

"You're not playing music. You're executing it." She crossed to the piano. "Seven letters, Jackie. I stopped counting after that."

Jackie stood. "Patty, I'm sorry. I was—things got busy. My father wanted me to focus on college prep, classical competitions—"

"You don't need to explain. I can see what happened here." She looked at the piano, the equipment, the perfection. "You're playing for approval now. Not for breath."

Jackie's jaw tightened. "You don't know what it's like. The pressure, the expectations—"

"You're right. I don't know what it's like in your house." She gestured at the studio. "But I know what it's like to make music that matters. We did it together. Remember?"

"Tomorrow night, I'm entering the Battle." She headed for the stairs. "Not to fix you. Not to make you friends again. To show you what you're missing."

"Patty—"

She climbed the stairs. Stopped halfway.

"At camp, when we harmonized, you said it felt like flying. Remember that? You said classical music was your father's language, but rock was yours. You said playing Queen made you feel like you could breathe."

Jackie stood frozen at the piano.

"Tomorrow night," Patty said, "I'll be breathing. While you and Nick suffocate in the roles you've chosen, I'll be reminding everyone what air tastes like."

She left. Elizabeth was waiting at the top of the stairs.

"Did you fix him?" the girl asked.

"No. You can't fix people who don't want to be fixed."

"Then why did you come?"

Patty looked back down the stairs. Jackie was sitting at the piano again, staring at nothing.

"Because someone has to show them what they're missing."

---

St. Michael's Church. Evening.

Patty sat alone in the sanctuary, the cassette tape ((another tape, don't like it)) on the pew beside her.

Tomorrow night, she'd walk onto that stage in Sudbury. Outsider in a war she hadn't started. Witness to a tragedy she couldn't stop. ((good!))

She wasn't going to fix Nick and Jackie. The labyrinth had them now. Class warfare, parental pressure, grief, pride—all the machinery of division grinding friendship into dust.((good))

But she could do what Maxanne Sartori had done with Aerosmith, with The Cars, with Boston. Play music that mattered. Music that didn't compete. Music that told the truth. ((I would leave MAxanne out here, too convenient not believable from Patty))

Nick and Jackie would be on that stage trying to prove they were better than each other. She'd be there proving music didn't care about better. It only cared about real. ((okay))

Patty sat alone in the sanctuary, listening to the silence.

But she could show them what music looked like when you weren't trying to prove anything. When you were just playing because it made you alive.

Nick and Jackie would be on that stage trying to prove they were better than each other. She'd be there proving music didn't care about better. It only cared about real.

They'd been real once. Three kids by a lake, making something beautiful because it was possible. Before they learned to compete instead of collaborate.

Tomorrow night, she'd remind everyone what possible looked like. What music sounded like before it became a weapon.

Not to save them. They were already lost.

Just to show them what they were missing.

The church was quiet except for the sound of her breathing.

Tomorrow, she'd make them listen. To what they'd thrown away. To what harmony cost when you chose competition instead.

And then she'd leave them with their choice.

Because that's all she could do. Show them what they were missing. Refuse to let them pretend it never existed.

Tomorrow night, the Battle of the Bands would crown a winner.

But Patty knew the truth: They'd already lost. All of them. The day friendship became competition.

She was just there to show them what winning looked like when you didn't care about winning.
